On these, then, will come [[2:8|wrath|ira]], that is, divine vengeance, [[2:8|and indignation|et indignatio]], that is, the abhorrence with which the eternal Judge will despise them, [[2:9|Tribulation|tribulatio]] of body, [[2:9|and anguish|et angustia]] of mind: these, I say, will come [[2:9|upon every soul of man that worketh evil|in omnem animam hominis operantis malum]], unless he repent (for the punishment of the body also overflows into the soul, and conversely), [[2:9|of the Jew first|Judæi primum]], that is, chiefly, since because of the divine law given him he sinned more gravely and will be punished more heavily, [[2:9|and also of the Greek|et Græci]]. If by Greeks is understood that particular nation, then the Greek is named after the Jew because more than the other nations he sinned and was punished, since he shone in natural philosophy and subtlety of wit. For where the gift of knowledge is greater, there the transgressor is subject to a heavier fault and punishment. But if by the Greek are understood the Gentiles in common, then the Greek is placed after the Jew because he sinned less, speaking in general and other things being equal.

paras.t: His verbis Apostoli consonat illud Proverbiorum quod ex persona æternæ Sapientiæ dicitur: Quia vocavi et renuistis, et extendi manum meam, et non fuit qui aspiceret, et despexistis omne consilium meum, et increpationes meas neglexistis, ego[…] quoque in interitu vestro ridebo, quum irruerit repentina calamitas, et interitus quasi tempestas ingruerit, quando venerit super vos tribulatio et angustia. Hoc loco Apostolus contentiosos redarguit. Unde de et Jacobus apostolus dicit : Si zelum amarum habetis, et contentiones sunt inter vos, nolite gloriari, et mendaces esse adversus veritatem. Denique tanta est culpa contentionis, ut propter ipsam corporalis exercitatio reprobetur, dicente Domino per Prophetam : Ecce ad lites et contentiones jejunatis : numquid tale est jejunium quod elegi?
paras.en: With these words of the Apostle agrees that of Proverbs, which is said in the person of the eternal Wisdom: [[Prov 1:24|Because I called, and you refused: I stretched out my hand, and there was none that regarded|Quia vocavi et renuistis, et extendi manum meam, et non fuit qui aspiceret]], [[Prov 1:25|You have despised all my counsel, and have neglected my reprehensions|despexistis omne consilium meum, et increpationes meas neglexistis]], [[Prov 1:26|I also will laugh in your destruction|ego quoque in interitu vestro ridebo]], [[Prov 1:27|When sudden calamity shall fall on you, and destruction, as a tempest, shall be at hand: when tribulation and distress shall come upon you|quum irruerit repentina calamitas, et interitus quasi tempestas ingruerit, quando venerit super vos tribulatio et angustia]]. In this place the Apostle rebukes the contentious. Hence James the apostle too says: [[Jas 3:14|But if you have bitter zeal, and there be contention in your hearts: glory not and be not liars against the truth|Si zelum amarum habetis, et contentiones sunt inter vos, nolite gloriari, et mendaces esse adversus veritatem]]. Lastly, so great is the fault of contention that because of it even bodily discipline is rejected, as the Lord says through the Prophet: [[Is 58:4|Behold you fast for debates and strife|Ecce ad lites et contentiones jejunatis]]: [[Is 58:5|Is this such a fast as I have chosen|numquid tale est jejunium quod elegi?]]?

paras.t: Gloria autem et honor, de quibus jam dictum est, et pax, id est tranquillitas mentis, seu securitas ab impugnatione hostili, dabuntur pro præmio omni operanti bonum ex caritate, Judæo primum, id est præcipue : quia in genere plus aliis meruerunt Judæi ad Christum conversi, videlicet sancti Apostoli, ac primitiva Ecclesia; et Græco, id est gentilibus.
paras.en: [[2:10|But glory and honour|Gloria autem et honor]], of which we have already spoken, [[2:10|and peace|et pax]], that is, tranquillity of mind, or security from the enemy's attack, will be given as a reward [[2:10|to every one that worketh good|omni operanti bonum]] out of charity, [[2:10|to the Jew first|Judæo primum]], that is, chiefly: because in general the Jews converted to Christ, namely the holy Apostles and the early Church, merited more than others; [[2:10|and also to the Greek|et Græco]], that is, to the Gentiles.

paras.t: Non est enim acceptio personarum apud Deum : id est, Deus in judicando non attendit personam, et ea quæ non habent rationem meriti sive demeriti, sed sola opera pensat, et unumquemque secundum merita sua judicat. Propter quod asserebat Petrus : In veritate comperi quoniam non est personarum acceptor Deus; sed in omni gente, qui timet Deum et operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi. Et per Prophetam Dominus loquitur : Unumquemque juxta vias suas judicabo. Ad hanc perfectionem hortatur nos sermo divinus, per Moysen dicens : Juste judicabis, nec consideres personam pauperis, neque honores vultum potentis.
paras.en: [[2:11|For there is no respect of persons with God|Non est enim acceptio personarum apud Deum]]: that is, God in judging does not regard the person, and those things which have no ground of merit or demerit, but weighs the works alone, and judges each according to his merits. For which reason Peter declared: [[Acts 10:34|in very deed I perceive that God is not a respecter of persons|In veritate comperi quoniam non est personarum acceptor Deus]]; [[Acts 10:35|But in every nation, he that feareth him and worketh justice is acceptable to him|sed in omni gente, qui timet Deum et operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi]]. And through the Prophet the Lord says: [[Ezech 33:20|I will judge every one of you according to his ways|Unumquemque juxta vias suas judicabo]]. To this perfection the divine word exhorts us, saying through Moses: [[Lev 19:15|Respect not the person of the poor: nor honour the countenance of the mighty|nec consideres personam pauperis, neque honores vultum potentis]] [Denis begins, "Thou shalt judge justly"].

paras.t: Porro, quod apud Deum non sit personarum acceptio, sed justum judicium, probat. Quicumque enim sine lege scripta atque Mosaica peccaverunt, videlicet non habendo legem, id est gentiles qui peccatum commiserunt, non quia legem scriptam transgressi sunt, quia nec eam habuerunt, sine lege peribunt, id est, non propter hujus legis prævaricationem damnabuntur, sed propter hoc quod legem naturalem non servaverunt cum fide Salvatoris saltem implicita, ut plenius ostendetur. Quum autem dicat Ambrosius, Peccatum est prævaricatio legis divinæ, quæri potest, quomodo aliquis peccare valeat sine lege. Et respondendum, quod in definitione Ambrosii, per legem divinam intelligitur quælibet lex data a Deo, a quo constat naturalem legem fluxisse, datamque esse. Et quicumque in lege scripta peccaverunt, eam non observando, sicut Judæi, per legem, id est ex ipsa lege scripta, vel propter legis transgressionem, judicabuntur judicio reprobationis. Unde Christus aiebat Judæis : Est qui accusat vos Moyses, in quo vos speratis.
paras.en: Further, he proves that with God there is no respect of persons, but just judgment. [[2:12|For whosoever have sinned without the law|Quicumque enim sine lege peccaverunt]], the written law of Moses, namely by not having the law, that is, the Gentiles who committed sin, not because they transgressed the written law, since they did not have it, [[2:12|shall perish without the law|sine lege peribunt]], that is, they will be damned not for breaking this law, but because they did not keep the natural law with at least an implicit faith in the Saviour, as will be shown more fully. Now since Ambrose says, *Sin is the breaking of the divine law*, it may be asked how anyone can sin without the law. The answer is that in Ambrose's definition by divine law is understood any law given by God, from whom it is certain the natural law flowed and was given. [[2:12|and whosoever have sinned in the law|Et quicumque in lege scripta peccaverunt]], the written law, by not keeping it, as the Jews, [[2:12|shall be judged by the law|per legem judicabuntur]], that is, from the written law itself, or for transgressing the law, with the judgment of reprobation. Hence Christ said to the Jews: [[John 5:45|There is one that accuseth you, Moses, in whom you trust|Est qui accusat vos Moyses, in quo vos speratis]].

paras.t: Non enim auditores legis divinitus datæ, justi sunt apud Deum, nisi obediant legi : ideo subditur, sed factores legis, id est, qui legis mandata adimplent, justificabuntur, id est, justi erunt ac reputabuntur apud Deum. Nam et fides sine operibus mortua est. Et in Evangelio Christus testatur : Omnis qui audit verba hæc, et non facit ea, assimilabitur viro stulto qui ædificavit domum suam supra arenam; et alibi, Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud. Ipsa ergo impletio legis per gratiam, ex qua procedit impletio, justificat hominem, estque justificatio ejus.
paras.en: [[2:13|For not the hearers of the law|Non enim auditores legis]] given by God [[2:13|are just before God|justi sunt apud Deum]], unless they obey the law: therefore it is added, [[2:13|but the doers of the law|sed factores legis]], that is, those who fulfil the commandments of the law, [[2:13|shall be justified|justificabuntur]], that is, will be, and be accounted, just before God. For [[Jas 2:20|faith without works is dead|fides sine operibus mortua est]]. And in the Gospel Christ testifies: [[Matt 7:26|And every one that heareth these my words and doth them not, shall be like a foolish man that built his house upon the sand|Omnis qui audit verba hæc, et non facit ea, assimilabitur viro stulto qui ædificavit domum suam supra arenam]]; and elsewhere, [[Luke 11:28|blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it|Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud]]. The very fulfilling of the law, then, through grace, from which the fulfilling proceeds, justifies a man, and is his justification.

paras.t: Denique, quod ipsa observatio legis justificet, elucescit ex hoc : Quum enim gentes, id est gentiles, quæ legem scriptam seu Moysis non habent, quia non tenebantur ad eam, naturaliter, id est ex naturalis rationis dictamine, adjuti tamen lumine gratiæ, sine qua nemo unquam salvatus est : non enim ex puris naturalibus quisquam salvatur, quum salus nostra sit supernaturalis felicitas, scilicet visio per speciem, ad quam sine fide, caritate et gratia Dei nullus viator pertingit; ea quæ legis sunt faciunt, id est, legem scriptam observant, quantum ad præcepta moralia Decalogi, quæ sunt de dictamine rationis naturalis; ejusmo di gentes legem Mosaicam non habentes, ipsi sibi sunt lex, id est, propria ratio est eis pro lege; qui ostendunt, bene vivendo, opus legis, quod a lege scripta præcipitur fieri aut vitari, scriptum in cordibus suis, id est intellectu naturali impressum : ita quod ratio dictat eis quod dictat lex scripta. Dum enim non faciunt alteri quod sibi nolunt fieri, quod utique naturalis ratio dictat, implent ea quæ jubet lex scripta. Nam et secundum Apostolum, Qui diligit proximum, legem implevit.
paras.en: Lastly, that the very keeping of the law justifies is made clear from this: [[2:14|For when the Gentiles|Quum enim gentes]], that is, the heathen, [[2:14|who have not the law|quæ legem non habent]], the written law of Moses, since they were not bound to it, [[2:14|do by nature|naturaliter]], that is, by the dictate of natural reason, helped however by the light of grace, without which no one has ever been saved (for no one is saved from pure nature alone, since our salvation is a supernatural happiness, namely vision by sight, which no wayfarer reaches without faith, charity and the grace of God), [[2:14|those things that are of the law|ea quæ legis sunt faciunt]], that is, keep the written law as to the moral precepts of the Decalogue, which are of the dictate of natural reason; [[2:14|these, having not the law|ejusmodi … legem … non habentes]], Gentiles of this kind not having the law of Moses, [[2:14|are a law to themselves|ipsi sibi sunt lex]], that is, their own reason is law for them; [[2:15|Who shew the work of the law|qui ostendunt, bene vivendo, opus legis]] by living well, the work which the written law commands to be done or avoided, [[2:15|written in their hearts|scriptum in cordibus suis]], that is, impressed on the natural understanding: so that reason dictates to them what the written law dictates. For when they do not do to another what they would not have done to themselves[[Tob 4:16||]][[Matt 7:12||]], which natural reason surely dictates, they fulfil what the written law commands. For according to the Apostle too, [[Rom 13:8|he that loveth his neighbour hath fulfilled the law|Qui diligit proximum, legem implevit]].

paras.t: Hi ergo qui naturaliter agunt ea quæ legis sunt, sibi sunt lex : quod declarat Apostolus per effectum, videlicet per conscientiæ testimonium. Subditur enim, testimonium boni vel mali reddente illis conscientia ipsorum, quæ ex naturali judicio rationis reprobat malum, et approbat bonum : recalcitrat enim quodammodo operi vitioso, consentitque actui virtuoso; et inter se invicem cogitationum accusantium, aut etiam defendentium. More Græcorum ponit genitivum pro ablativo, ut sit sensus : Cogitationibus se invicem accusantibus, id est perversis cogitationibus quæ malos accusant, aut etiam defendentibus, id est cogitationibus bonis quæ bonos excusant atque defendunt : his, inquam, cogitationibus testimonium damnationis vel salutis reddentibus illis, id est prædictis gentilibus. Istæ cogitationes accusantes ac defendentes, hoc est malæ ac bonæ, examinantur, dijudicantur et declarantur coram naturali judicatorio hominis, quasi coram judice, per prima agibilium principia naturaliter inserta et cognita, sicut est illud : Quod tibi vis fieri, fac alteri. Quamvis autem testimonium istud modo reddat conscientia, tamen in futuro extremo judicio clarius perhibebit. Tunc namque quilibet conscius erit sibi de propriis bonis ac malis. Ideirco subjungitur, in die quum judicabit Deus occulta hominum, id est in die judicii, quando aperientur conscientiarum libri, secundum evan[…]lium meum, id est secundum quod ego evangelizo ac prædico. Evangelium enim est Christi, tanquam auctoris ; Joannis vero, Matthæi, Lucæ, et Marci, tanquam scriptorum; Pauli autem et aliorum Apostolorum, tanquam prædicatorum. Quod vero mox subditur, per Jesum Christum, referri potest ad illud quod dictum est, Judicabit Deus, etc., quia per Christum hominem exercebitur illud judicium, ita quod ipse ut homo erit exsecutor judicii (Pater enim non judicat quemquam, sed judicium omne dedit Filio); vel ad illud quod dictum est, Secundum evangelium meum. Per Christum enim factum est evangelium Pauli, sicut superius ait : Per quem accepimus gratiam et apostolatum.
paras.en: These, then, who by nature do the things of the law are a law to themselves: which the Apostle makes plain by the effect, namely by the witness of conscience. For it is added, [[2:15|their conscience bearing witness to them|testimonium reddente illis conscientia ipsorum]] of good or evil, the conscience which by the natural judgment of reason rejects evil and approves good: for it kicks back in a manner against a vicious work, and consents to a virtuous act; [[2:15|and their thoughts between themselves accusing or also defending one another|et inter se invicem cogitationum accusantium, aut etiam defendentium]]. In the manner of the Greeks he puts the genitive for the ablative, so that the sense is: their thoughts accusing one another, that is, the perverse thoughts which accuse the wicked, or also defending, that is, the good thoughts which excuse and defend the good: these thoughts, I say, bearing them witness of damnation or salvation, that is, to the Gentiles spoken of. These accusing and defending thoughts, that is, bad and good, are examined, judged and declared before the natural judgment-seat of man, as before a judge, by the first principles of action naturally implanted and known, such as that, [[Matt 7:12|whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do you also to them|Quod tibi vis fieri, fac alteri]] [Denis gives the saying in the common form, "What you would have done to you, do to another"]. And although conscience bears this witness now, yet in the last judgment to come it will bear it more clearly. For then each one will be conscious to himself of his own good and evil. Therefore it is added, [[2:16|In the day when God shall judge the secrets of men|in die quum judicabit Deus occulta hominum]], that is, on the day of judgment, when the books of consciences will be opened, [[2:16|according to my gospel|secundum evangelium meum]], that is, according to what I preach as the gospel. For the Gospel is Christ's as its author; John's, Matthew's, Luke's and Mark's as its writers; and Paul's and the other Apostles' as its preachers. And what is added at once, [[2:16|by Jesus Christ|per Jesum Christum]], may be referred to what was said, *God shall judge*, etc., because that judgment will be carried out by Christ as man, so that he as man will be the executor of the judgment (for [[John 5:22|neither does the Father judge any man: but hath given all judgment to the Son|Pater enim non judicat quemquam, sed judicium omne dedit Filio]]); or to what was said, *according to my gospel*. For through Christ the gospel of Paul came about, as he said above: [[Rom 1:5|By whom we have received grace and apostleship|Per quem accepimus gratiam et apostolatum]].

paras.t: Potest quoque ita exponi : Testimonium illis reddente conscientia ipsorum, id est conscientia operum; nec solum conscientia operum, sed et conscientia cogitationum inter se invicem accusantium aut defendentium, juxta sensum præhabitum. Dicit autem glossator, quod in die judicii cogitationes accusabunt animam vel defendent, non quæ tunc erunt, sed quæ nunc sunt in nobis : quarum quædam notæ atque signacula relinquuntur in corde nostro, velut in cera, quæ in occulto nunc pectoris posita, tunc revelari dicuntur per Christum. Sed contra ire huic videtur quod ait Anselmus, et alii Sancti, quod etiam certum est, scilicet quod in die judicii erit in reprobis conscientia urens atque remordens, in electis vero conscientia bonæ fiduciæ. Omnium enim opera cunctis patebunt. Sciendum ergo, quod cogitationes quæ nunc sunt, tunc accusabunt vel defendent per modum meriti sive demeriti. Cogitationes vero quæ tunc erunt, accusabunt aut defendent, non per modum meriti vel demeriti, quia non erit tunc locus merendi aut demerendi quum via sit finita, sed tanquam signa præteritorum meritorum aut demeritorum. Et sic glossator salvatur per distinctionem.
paras.en: It may also be expounded thus: *their conscience bearing witness to them*, that is, the conscience of their works; and not only the conscience of works, but also the conscience of their thoughts accusing or defending one another, in the sense given before. And the glossator says that on the day of judgment the thoughts will accuse or defend the soul, not those that will be then, but those that are in us now: of which certain marks and seals are left in our heart, as in wax, which, laid up now in the hidden place of the breast, are said to be revealed then through Christ. But against this seems to go what Anselm and other saints say, which is also certain, namely that on the day of judgment there will be in the reprobate a conscience burning and gnawing, and in the elect a conscience of good confidence. For the works of all will be open to all. We must know, then, that the thoughts that are now will then accuse or defend by way of merit or demerit; but the thoughts that will be then will accuse or defend, not by way of merit or demerit, since there will then be no place for meriting or demeriting, the way being ended, but as signs of past merits or demerits. And so the glossator is saved by a distinction.

paras.t: Consequenter Apostolus Judæos aggreditur, probans eos, quantum ad aliquid, deteriores gentilibus. Quo enim plura beneficia atque auxilia contra peccatum receperunt, eo gravius peccaverunt in eodem genere culpæ : quia quo status sublimior, eo ruina est major. Denique excellentia status Judæorum fuit in hoc, quod legem divinam, præcepta moralia, judicialia ac cærimonialia, diversaque alia gratiarum munera receperunt. Unde Moyses loquebatur : Quæ est alia gens sic inclyta, ut habeat cærimonias, justaque judicia, et universam legem, ut populus tuus, Israel? Ipsi vero ingrati Deo fuerunt. Propter quod Dominus conqueritur per Prophetam : Filios, inquiens, enutrivi et exaltavi, ipsi autem spreverunt me. His ergo nunc ait Apostolus :
paras.en: Next the Apostle attacks the Jews, proving them in some respect worse than the Gentiles. For the more benefits and helps against sin they received, the more grievously they sinned in the same kind of fault: since the higher the state, the greater the fall. Lastly, the excellence of the state of the Jews lay in this, that they received the divine law, the moral, judicial and ceremonial precepts, and various other gifts of grace. Hence Moses said: [[Deut 4:8|For what other nation is there so renowned that hath ceremonies, and just judgments, and all the law|Quæ est alia gens sic inclyta, ut habeat cærimonias, justaque judicia, et universam legem]], as thy people, Israel? But they were ungrateful to God. For which reason the Lord complains through the Prophet: [[Is 1:2|I have brought up children, and exalted them: but they have despised me|Filios, inquiens, enutrivi et exaltavi, ipsi autem spreverunt me]] (he says). To these, then, the Apostle now says:

paras.t: Si autem, id est quia, tu Judæus cognominaris a Juda patriarcha, qui inter fratres suos fortissimus erat, ut dicit Scriptura. Primo siquidem appellati sunt Hebræi ab Heber, in quo remansit lingua Hebraica, quæ ante constructionem turris Babylonicæ omnibus erat communis, juxta illud : Erat autem terra labii unius. Postmodum dicti sunt Israelitæ a Jacob, qui vocatus est Israel. Tertio dicti sunt Judæi a Juda. Hoc tamen nomine specialiter vocabantur duæ tribus. Nam Israel dictæ sunt aliæ decem tribus, a tempore separationis suæ a domo David. Et requiescis, id est persistis, in lege Mosaica, non evagando per diversos errores more gentilium, et gloriaris in Deo, id est in cognitione ipsius, et nosti voluntatem ejus ex doctrina legis ac Prophetarum, et probas, id est, approbas seu commendas, utiliora, id est perfectiora et viciniora saluti, instructus per legem, in qua diversi gradus perfectionum docentur; confidis, id est, præsumis et æstimas, te ipsum ducem esse cæcorum, id est tantæ perfectionis, ut aliis spiritualiter excæcatis possis viam virtutis ostendere, eosque in via Dei præcedere, atque ad rectum finem perducere; confidis quoque te lumen esse eorum qui in tenebris ignorantiæ sunt, id est tantæ gratiæ ac scientiæ, ut ignorantes valeas illustrare, eruditorem insipientium, id est divinorum cognitione carentium, scilicet infidelium, quos Judæi sæpe converterunt ad Deum, magistrum infantium, hoc est parvulorum seu imperfectorum, qui solidum cibum capere non valentes, expertes sunt sermonis justitiæ, habentem formam, id est perfectionem aliis exemplarem, scientiæ in agendis, et veritatis in lege, id est in credendis ac speculativis.
paras.en: [[2:17|But if thou art called a Jew|Si autem tu Judæus cognominaris]], *if*, that is, since, from Juda the patriarch, who [[1 Par 5:2|was the strongest among his brethren|inter fratres suos fortissimus erat]], as Scripture says. For first they were called Hebrews from Heber[[Gen 10:21||]], in whom the Hebrew tongue remained, which before the building of the tower of Babel was common to all, according to that: [[Gen 11:1|And the earth was of one tongue|Erat autem terra labii unius]]. Afterwards they were called Israelites from Jacob, who was called Israel[[Gen 32:28||]][[Gen 35:10||]]. Thirdly they were called Jews from Juda. Yet by this name two tribes were called in a special way: for the other ten tribes were called Israel, from the time of their separation from the house of David[[3 Kings 12:19||]]. [[2:17|and restest|Et requiescis]], that is, abide, [[2:17|in the law|in lege]] of Moses, not wandering through various errors after the manner of the Gentiles, [[2:17|and makest thy boast of God|et gloriaris in Deo]], that is, in the knowledge of him, [[2:18|And knowest his will|et nosti voluntatem ejus]] from the teaching of the law and the Prophets, [[2:18|and approvest|et probas]], that is, commend, [[2:18|the more profitable things|utiliora]], that is, the more perfect and nearer to salvation, [[2:18|being instructed by the law|instructus per legem]], in which various degrees of perfection are taught; [[2:19|Art confident|confidis]], that is, presume and think, [[2:19|that thou thyself art a guide of the blind|te ipsum ducem esse cæcorum]], that is, of such perfection that you can show the way of virtue to others who are spiritually blinded, and go before them in the way of God, and lead them to the right end; you are confident also that you are [[2:19|a light of them that are in darkness|lumen … eorum qui in tenebris … sunt]] of ignorance, that is, of such grace and knowledge that you can enlighten the ignorant, [[2:20|An instructor of the foolish|eruditorem insipientium]], that is, of those lacking the knowledge of divine things, namely unbelievers, whom the Jews often converted to God, [[2:20|a teacher of infants|magistrum infantium]], that is, of little ones or the imperfect, who, not being able to take solid food, are unskilful in the word of justice[[Heb 5:12||]][[Heb 5:13||]], [[2:20|having the form|habentem formam]], that is, a perfection that is an example to others, [[2:20|of knowledge|scientiæ]] in what is to be done, [[2:20|and of truth in the law|et veritatis in lege]], that is, in what is to be believed and speculative matters.

paras.t: Porro, quod subditur, interrogative, admirative et increpative intelligendum est. Qui ergo alium doces, te ipsum non doces? id est, quum alium docere præsumas, cur te ipsum non doces? Et mirum est quod te ipsum non doces; et male agis, eo quod te ipsum non doceas. Simili modo legenda sunt quæ sequuntur. Qui prædicas non furandum, furaris? Qui dicis non mœchandum, mœcharis? Commiserunt autem Judæi et spirituale furtum ac mœchationem, subtrahendo a lege sensum de Christo ac mysticum intellectum. Qui abominaris idola, id est idololatriæ cultum, sacrilegium facis, id est furtum atque abusum rei sacræ? Aliqua enim divino cultui deputata, propriis usibus applicabant Judæi, quia avarissimi erant sacerdotes, Scribæ ac Pharisæi. Nam divina præcepta suis superstitiosis traditionibus irrita fecerunt, ut Evangelium loquitur. Qui in lege, id est de legis acceptione, gloriaris, dicendo, Quanta audivimus et cognovimus ea; et, Non fecit taliter omni nationi; per prævaricationem legis Deum inhonoras, non exhibendo ei reverentiam debitam, obediendo mandatis ipsius? Nomen enim Dei per vos, id est occasione vestri, blasphematur inter gentes, id est a gentibus perfidis, quæ videntes vestram perversitatem, Deum vestrum blasphemant, æstimantes eum injustum qui tales servos asseritur elegisse, sicut scriptum est in Ezechiele, ubi prædicta verba habentur secundum translationem Septuaginta interpretum. Nostra autem translatio talis est : Ingressi sunt ad gentes, et polluerunt nomen meum. Et sicut Ezechiel ista dicebat de Judæis sibi contemporaneis, ad quos missus erat, sic Paulus hæc applicat Judæis sui temporis.
paras.en: Further, what follows is to be understood as a question, with wonder and rebuke. [[2:21|Thou therefore, that teachest another, teachest not thyself|Qui ergo alium doces, te ipsum non doces?]] That is, since you presume to teach another, why do you not teach yourself? And it is strange that you do not teach yourself; and you do ill in not teaching yourself. In like manner are to be read the things that follow. [[2:21|thou, that preachest that men should not steal, stealest|Qui prædicas non furandum, furaris?]] [[2:22|Thou, that sayest men should not commit adultery, committest adultery|Qui dicis non mœchandum, mœcharis?]] And the Jews committed a spiritual theft and adultery as well, by withdrawing from the law its sense concerning Christ and its mystical understanding. [[2:22|thou, that abhorrest idols|Qui abominaris idola]], that is, the worship of idolatry, [[2:22|committest sacrilege|sacrilegium facis]], that is, theft and misuse of a sacred thing? For the Jews applied to their own uses some things set apart for divine worship, since the priests, Scribes and Pharisees were most covetous[[Luke 16:14||]]. For they made void the divine commandments by their superstitious traditions, as the Gospel says[[Matt 15:6||]]. [[2:23|Thou, that makest thy boast of the law|qui in lege gloriaris]], that is, of the receiving of the law, saying, [[Ps 77:3|How great things have we heard and known|Quanta audivimus et cognovimus ea]]; and, [[Ps 147:9|He hath not done in like manner to every nation|Non fecit taliter omni nationi]] [the margin gives Ps. cxlvii, 20, counting by the Hebrew]; [[2:23|by transgression of the law dishonourest God|per prævaricationem legis Deum inhonoras]], not showing him due reverence by obeying his commandments? [[2:24|For the name of God through you|Nomen enim Dei per vos]], that is, on your account, [[2:24|is blasphemed among the Gentiles|blasphematur inter gentes]], that is, by the faithless Gentiles, who, seeing your perversity, blaspheme your God, thinking him unjust who is declared to have chosen such servants, [[2:24|as it is written|sicut scriptum est]] in Ezechiel[[Ezech 36:20||]], where the words given above are found according to the translation of the Septuagint. But our translation reads thus: [[Ezech 36:20|when they entered among the nations whither they went, they profaned my holy name|Ingressi sunt ad gentes, et polluerunt nomen meum]]. And as Ezechiel said these things of the Jews of his own time, to whom he was sent, so Paul applies them to the Jews of his time.

paras.t: Subinde ostendit Apostolus gravitatem excessus Judæorum ex conditione circumcisionis. Circumcisio namque erat signum justitiæ, et quædam professio legis servandæ, juxta illud Apostoli ad Galatas : Testificor omni homini circumcidenti se, quod debitor sit universæ legis faciendæ. Quemadmodum ergo nunc prodest professio vitæ claustralis, si regula observetur ; si vero regula omittatur, plurimum obest, et peccatum gravatur : sic de circumcisione erat tempore veteris Testamenti. Hoc est quod Apostolus subjungit.
paras.en: Next the Apostle shows the gravity of the Jews' excess from the condition of circumcision. For circumcision was a sign of justice, and a kind of profession that the law would be kept, according to that of the Apostle to the Galatians: [[Gal 5:3|I testify again to every man circumcising himself that he is a debtor to do the whole law|Testificor omni homini circumcidenti se, quod debitor sit universæ legis faciendæ]]. As, then, the profession of the cloistered life profits now if the rule is kept, but if the rule is neglected it does very great harm and the sin is made heavier: so it was with circumcision in the time of the Old Testament. This is what the Apostle adds.

paras.t: Circumcisio quidem prodest ad gratiam promerendam, videlicet tempore veteris Testamenti, non autem Evangelio divulgato, si legem observes. Si autem prævaricator legis Mosaicæ sis, circumcisio tua carnalis præputium facta est, id est præputio similis, non plus valens quam illud. Si ergo præputium, id est gentilis incircumcisus, justitias legis, id est præcepta moralia, quæ sunt de dictamine rationis naturalis, custodiat cum fide et cultu unius Dei, ut tactum est, nonne præputium illius in circumcisionem reputabitur, id est, tantum sibi proficiet ad salutem, ut tibi, o Judæe, circumcisio tua? quasi dicat, Ita. Custodiendo enim justitias legis modo præfato, spiritualiter circumciditur, et filius Abrahæ reputatur. Et judicabit id quod ex natura est præputium, id est gentilis præputium naturaliter habens, ex gentilibus ortus et in præputio natus, legem consummans, hoc est, justitias legis scriptæ adimplens ex naturali dictamine rationis : judicabit, inquam, id est, sui comparatione judicio damnationis dignum ostendet, […] Judæe. qui per litteram, id est legis scripturam, et circumcisionem prævaricator legis es, id est, nec per Scripturam sacram, neque per circumcisionis significationem a peccato retraheris, a quo gentilis retrahitur per legem naturalem sine circumcisione ac littera Scripturarum?
paras.en: [[2:25|Circumcision profiteth indeed|Circumcisio quidem prodest]] for meriting grace, namely in the time of the Old Testament, but not once the Gospel has been published, [[2:25|if thou keep the law|si legem observes]]. [[2:25|but if thou be a transgressor of the law|Si autem prævaricator legis Mosaicæ sis]] of Moses, [[2:25|thy circumcision is made uncircumcision|circumcisio tua carnalis præputium facta est]] in the flesh, that is, like uncircumcision, worth no more than it. [[2:26|If then, the uncircumcised|Si ergo præputium]], that is, the uncircumcised Gentile, [[2:26|keep the justices of the law|justitias legis custodiat]], that is, the moral precepts, which are of the dictate of natural reason, with faith in and worship of the one God, as has been touched on, [[2:26|shall not this uncircumcision be counted for circumcision|nonne præputium illius in circumcisionem reputabitur]], that is, will it not profit him as much for salvation as your circumcision does you, O Jew? As if he were saying: So it is. For by keeping the justices of the law in the way mentioned he is spiritually circumcised, and is reckoned a son of Abraham. [[2:27|And shall not that which by nature is uncircumcision|Et judicabit id quod ex natura est præputium]], that is, the Gentile having uncircumcision by nature, born of Gentiles and in uncircumcision, [[2:27|if it fulfil the law|legem consummans]], that is, fulfilling the justices of the written law from the natural dictate of reason, [[2:27|judge thee|judicabit]], I say, that is, by comparison with himself show you worthy of the judgment of damnation, […] O Jew, [[2:27|who by the letter and circumcision art a transgressor of the law|qui per litteram et circumcisionem prævaricator legis es?]], that is, who are not drawn back from sin either by holy Scripture or by the meaning of circumcision, from which the Gentile is drawn back by the natural law without circumcision and the letter of the Scriptures?

paras.t: Quod autem gentilis juste vivens, melior est Judæo circumciso injuste vivente, et eum condemnet, probat Apostolus, eo quod duplex sit circumcisio, scilicet spiritualis, et carnalis. Quarum prima facit spiritualem Judæum, secunda carnalem. Unde Propheta : Omnes, inquit, gentes habent præputium, omnis autem domus Israel incircumcisi sunt corde. Ad spiritualem vero circumcisionem admonet Moyses : Circumcidite, inquiens, præputium cordis vestri, et cervicem vestram ne induretis amplius. Et quantum caro est inferior spiritu, tantum circumcisio carnalis et carnalis Judæus inferiores sunt spirituali circumcisione atque Judæo. Ait itaque: Non enim qui in manifesto, id est, qui circumcisus est carne, et potest hominibus signum Judaismi ostendere, Judæus est solum et vere : Judæus enim interpretatur confitens, quod competit non solum circumciso ; neque quæ in manifesto, in carne, est circumcisio, id est, circumcisio illa exterior pelliculam tollens, est circumcisio perfecta ac vera. Sed qui in abscondito, id est, qui corde circumcisus est (quæ circumcisio homines latet, Deoque patet), Judæus est vere ac spiritualiter, confitens Domino confessione laudis divinæ : […] […] dis, id est circumcisio spiritualis facta in spiritu, id est secundum spiritualem intellectum Scripturæ veteris Testamenti, non littera, id est non secundum sensum litteralem ipsius ; vel, In spiritu, id est virtute Spiritus Sancti, non littera, id est litteralibus cultris legis. Cujus, videlicet spiritualis circumcisionis, laus non […] ex hominibus, qui in interiori loco non valent, neque de eis certum quidquam […] judicant, sed […] qui inspector […]
paras.en: And that the Gentile who lives justly is better than the circumcised Jew who lives unjustly, and condemns him, the Apostle proves from this, that circumcision is twofold, namely spiritual and carnal. The first of these makes the spiritual Jew, the second the carnal. Hence the Prophet says: [[Jer 9:26|all the nations are uncircumcised in the flesh, but all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart|Omnes, inquit, gentes habent præputium, omnis autem domus Israel incircumcisi sunt corde]] [Denis has "all nations have the foreskin"]. And Moses admonishes to spiritual circumcision: [[Deut 10:16|Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and stiffen your neck no more|Circumcidite, inquiens, præputium cordis vestri, et cervicem vestram ne induretis amplius]] (he says). And as much as the flesh is lower than the spirit, so much are carnal circumcision and the carnal Jew lower than the spiritual circumcision and the spiritual Jew. He says, therefore: [[2:28|For it is not he is a Jew, who is so outwardly|Non enim qui in manifesto, Judæus est]], that is, he who is circumcised in the flesh and can show men the sign of Judaism is not only and truly a Jew: for *Jew* means one who confesses [praises], which belongs not only to the circumcised; [[2:28|nor is that circumcision which is outwardly in the flesh|neque quæ in manifesto, in carne, est circumcisio]], that is, that outward circumcision which removes a little skin is not perfect and true circumcision. [[2:29|But he is a Jew that is one inwardly|sed qui in abscondito, Judæus est]], that is, he who is circumcised in heart (which circumcision is hidden from men and open to God) is truly and spiritually a Jew, confessing the Lord with the confession of divine praise: […] [[2:29|and the circumcision is that of the heart|circumcisio]] [the transcription is unreadable here], that is, the spiritual circumcision made [[2:29|in the spirit|in spiritu]], that is, according to the spiritual understanding of the Scripture of the Old Testament, [[2:29|not in the letter|non littera]], that is, not according to its literal sense; or, *in the spirit*, that is, by the power of the Holy Ghost, *not in the letter*, that is, by the literal knives of the law. [[2:29|whose praise is not of men|Cujus … laus non … ex hominibus]], namely of the spiritual circumcision, who cannot reach the inward place, nor […] judge anything certain about them, but […] who, the searcher [… the rest of this sentence is unreadable in the transcription].

1.t: Quoniam itaque digni sunt morte æterna, non solum qui peccata prædicta committunt, sed etiam quicumque consentiunt, vel quum possint, non impediunt : Propter quod inexcusabilis es a peccato, o homo omnis qui judicas, id est, damnas seu reprobas alium, non secundum ordinem æquitatis ac regulas juris, sed inordinato judicio. In quo enim alterum judicas hoc modo, te ipsum condemnas, id est, damnatione dignum ostendis ac profiteris. Juxta quem sensum scriptum est : Dum maledicit impius diabolum, maledicit ipse animam suam. Unde ait Salvator : Ex ore tuo te judico, serve nequam. Et alibi : Hoc tuum est judicium, quod ipse decrevisti.
1.en: Since, then, not only those who commit the sins mentioned are worthy of eternal death, but also whoever consent to them, or do not hinder them when they could[[Rom 1:32||]]: [[2:1|Wherefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest|Propter quod inexcusabilis es a peccato, o homo omnis qui judicas]] (inexcusable of sin), that is, condemn or reject another, not according to the order of equity and the rules of right, but by a disordered judgment. [[2:1|For wherein thou judgest another|In quo enim alterum judicas]] in this way, [[2:1|thou condemnest thyself|te ipsum condemnas]], that is, you show and profess yourself worthy of condemnation. In which sense it is written: [[Ecclus 21:30|While the ungodly curseth the devil, he curseth his own soul|Dum maledicit impius diabolum, maledicit ipse animam suam]]. Hence the Saviour says: [[Luke 19:22|Out of thy own mouth I judge thee, thou wicked servant|Ex ore tuo te judico, serve nequam]]. And elsewhere: [[3 Kings 20:40|This is thy judgment, which thyself hast decreed|Hoc tuum est judicium, quod ipse decrevisti]].

1.t: Verumtamen, quoniam sacra Scriptura frequenter hortatur nos ad judicandum (juxta illud Prophetæ : Indicabo tibi, homo, quid sit bonum, aut quid Dominus requirat a te : facere judicium; et infra dicit Apostolus : Spiritualis homo omnia judicat), frequenter quoque prohibet nos judicare, præsertim in hoc libro Epistolarum Pauli : ad agnoscendum ergo quomodo hæc omnia intelligi debeant, scire oportet quod judicium proprie sumptum est actus virtutis, videlicet determinatio juris seu definitio justi. Talis autem determinatio juris, est actus justitiæ : ideo judicium est actus justitiæ, tanquam inclinantis et disponentis judicantem, ut dignus atque idoneus sit ad judicandum. Actus namque virtutis ex virtute procedit. Nec potest bene judicare de operibus virtutis, qui habitum virtutis non habet. Unde castus bene judicat de pertinentibus ad castitatem, et fortis, de his quæ ad fortitudinem pertinent. Judicium tamen est actus rationis seu prudentiæ, tanquam dirigentis atque sententiam proferentis. In quantum itaque judicium procedit ex quadam connaturalitate judicantis ad judicata, requirit habitum virtutis in judicante.
1.en: However, since holy Scripture often exhorts us to judge (according to that of the Prophet, [[Mich 6:8|I will shew thee, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requireth of thee: Verily to do judgment|Indicabo tibi, homo, quid sit bonum, aut quid Dominus requirat a te : facere judicium]]; and further on the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 2:15|the spiritual man judgeth all things|Spiritualis homo omnia judicat]]), and often also forbids us to judge, especially in this book of the Epistles of Paul: to know, then, how all these things ought to be understood, we must know that judgment, properly taken, is an act of virtue, namely the determining of right, or the defining of what is just. Such a determining of right is an act of justice: therefore judgment is an act of justice, as the virtue that inclines and disposes the one judging so that he is worthy and fit to judge. For the act of a virtue proceeds from the virtue. Nor can he judge well of the works of a virtue who has not the habit of the virtue. Hence the chaste man judges well of what belongs to chastity, and the brave man of what belongs to fortitude. Yet judgment is an act of reason, or of prudence, as directing and pronouncing the sentence. Inasmuch, then, as judgment proceeds from a certain connaturality of the one judging with the things judged, it requires the habit of virtue in the one judging.

1.t: Quoniam ergo judicium actus justitiæ est, in tantum licitum perhibetur, in quantum ex justitia oritur. Ad hoc autem quod judicium sit actus justitiæ, tria sunt necessaria : primo, ut procedat ex inclinatione virtutis, non ex impetu passionis aut suspicionis; secundo, ut procedat ex auctoritate præsidentis; tertio, ut proferatur secundum rectam rationem prudentiæ. Quodcumque horum defuerit, erit inordinatum illicitumque judicium. Si etenim primum defuerit, vocatur perversum; si secundum, dicitur usurpatum; si tertium desit, temerarium appellatur. Unde Chrysostomus super Matthæum : Qui in magnis peccatis sunt, eos judicare non debent qui in eisdem peccatis aut certe minoribus sunt. Et hoc, secundum Thomam, potissimum verum est, quando peccata prælati aut judicis publica sunt, et quando non est necesse judicare de alio ratione officii. Si vero peccata occulta sint, et necesse sit judicare ratione injuncti officii, potest cum timore ac humilitate judicare sive arguere. Si autem peccata sint manifesta, et nihilo minus judicare oporteat, debet primo intra se pœnitere. Nobis vero diligenter pensandum est illud S. Ambrosii : Judicet de errore et culpa alterius, qui in se ipso non habet quod judicet, ne quum de alio judicat, in se ipsum ferat sententiam.
1.en: Since, then, judgment is an act of justice, it is declared lawful in so far as it springs from justice. And for judgment to be an act of justice, three things are necessary: first, that it proceed from the inclination of virtue, not from the impulse of passion or suspicion; secondly, that it proceed from the authority of one who presides; thirdly, that it be pronounced according to the right reason of prudence. Whichever of these is lacking, the judgment will be disordered and unlawful. For if the first is lacking, it is called perverse; if the second, usurped; if the third, it is called rash. Hence Chrysostom on Matthew: Those who are in great sins ought not to judge those who are in the same sins, or surely in lesser ones. And this, according to Thomas, is most of all true when the sins of the prelate or judge are public, and when there is no need to judge another by reason of office. But if the sins are hidden, and it is necessary to judge by reason of the office laid upon him, he may judge or reprove with fear and humility. And if the sins are manifest, and he must nevertheless judge, he ought first to repent within himself. And we must weigh carefully that saying of St Ambrose: Let him judge of another's error and fault who has nothing in himself to judge, lest when he judges another he pass sentence on himself.

1.t: De prædictis ergo inordinatis judiciis intelligenda sunt loca Scripturæ in quibus vetatur judicium : sicut quum dicitur, Nolite judicare, et non judicabimini. Potest autem et debet quilibet nostrum judicare, reprobare, et castigare se ipsum. In communi quoque possumus judicare de actibus atque generibus hominum, secundum doctrinam et determinationem Scripturæ : ut, quod omnis homicida damnabitur, et omnis superbia sit peccatum. Duo vero sunt in quibus, secundum Augustinum, vitare debemus judicium : Primo, quum ignoramus quo animo aliquid fiat. Idcirco de occultis ac dubiis judicare prohibemur. Secundo, dum ignoramus qualis futurus sit qui judicandus videtur. Et quia hoc semper ignoramus, non debemus absolute personam alterius judicare, præsertim quum ignoremus an dignus sit amore, an odio, possitque omni momento a Deo tangi, compungi, pœnitere, et purificari. De actibus tamen manifestis, et quæ animo bono fieri nequeunt, judicare permittimur, compatiendo potius quam spernendo.
1.en: Of the disordered judgments spoken of, then, are to be understood the places of Scripture in which judgment is forbidden: as when it is said, [[Luke 6:37|Judge not: and you shall not be judged|Nolite judicare, et non judicabimini]]. But each of us can and ought to judge, reprove and chastise himself. In general too we can judge of the acts and kinds of men according to the teaching and decision of Scripture: as that every murderer will be damned, and that all pride is sin. But there are two things, according to Augustine, in which we must avoid judgment. First, when we do not know with what mind something is done: therefore we are forbidden to judge of hidden and doubtful things. Secondly, when we do not know what he will be who seems to be judged. And since we never know this, we ought not to judge the person of another absolutely, especially since we do not know whether he is worthy of love or of hatred[[Eccles 9:1||]], and he may at any moment be touched by God, pricked to the heart, repent and be purified. Of acts that are manifest, however, and which cannot be done with a good mind, we are allowed to judge, with compassion rather than contempt.

1.t: Denique judicium duplex est, scilicet discretionis, quo inter bonum et malum discernitur, et remunerationis, quo de præmio sententiatur. Horum judiciorum utrumque laudabile est, servatis circumstantiis et conditionibus debitis. De judicio quippe discretionis Dominus loquitur per Prophetam : Si separaveris pretiosum a vili, quasi os meum eris. De quo in Job habetur : Judicium eligamus, et inter nos videamus quid sit melius; itemque, Numquid qui non amat judicium, potest sanari? Judicium autem remunerationis est duplex, videlicet approbationis, quantum ad bonos, et reprobationis, quantum ad malos.
1.en: Lastly, judgment is twofold, namely of discernment, by which good and evil are told apart, and of recompense, by which sentence is given about reward. Each of these judgments is praiseworthy, the due circumstances and conditions being kept. Of the judgment of discernment the Lord speaks through the Prophet: [[Jer 15:19|thou wilt separate the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth|Si separaveris pretiosum a vili, quasi os meum eris]]. Of which we have in Job: [[Job 34:4|Let us choose to us judgment, and let us see among ourselves what is the best|Judicium eligamus, et inter nos videamus quid sit melius]]; and again, [[Job 34:17|Can he be healed that loveth not judgment?|Numquid qui non amat judicium, potest sanari?]] And the judgment of recompense is twofold, namely of approval, as regards the good, and of reprobation, as regards the wicked.

1.t: Secundum quoque quod Paulus hoc loco ad litteram loquitur contra Ecclesiam Romanorum, quæ ex Judæis et gentilibus collecta erat, qui se mutuo judicabant. Judæus enim judicavit gentilem de transgressione legis naturalis, gentilis vero Judæum de prævaricatione legis divinæ. Quilibet vero istorum, secundum Apostolum, inexcusabilis est. Cujus ratio subditur. Eadem enim agis, hoc est, similia, vel eadem genere aut specie, tu Judæe, operaris, quæ in gentili judicas, id est redarguis atque condemnas; vel, eadem agis, tu gentilis, quæ in Judæo judicas. Hoc generaliter accipi potest de unoquoque nostrum qui de illo peccato alium judicat, quod ipse in se ipso non corrigit.
1.en: And according to the letter Paul is speaking here against the Church of the Romans, which was gathered from Jews and Gentiles, who judged one another. For the Jew judged the Gentile for transgressing the natural law, and the Gentile the Jew for breaking the divine law. And each of these, according to the Apostle, is inexcusable. The reason for this is added: [[2:1|For thou dost the same things|Eadem enim agis]], that is, like things, or the same in genus or species, you, Jew, do, [[2:1|which thou judgest|quæ in gentili judicas]] in the Gentile, that is, reprove and condemn; or, you, Gentile, do the same things that you judge in the Jew. This can be taken generally of each of us who judges another for a sin which he does not correct in himself.

1.t: Quod consequenter declarat Apostolus. Scimus enim per naturalem rationem, vel supernaturalem illuminationem, quoniam judicium Dei est secundum veritatem, id est secundum justitiam, qua reddit singulis quod merentur, hoc est, scimus quod judicium Dei sit justum, in eos, id est adversus eos, qui talia agunt, id est, se invicem temerarie judicant, sicut jam dictum est. Tales enim reprobat Deus. Circa quod Origenes sic ait : Illud hoc loco videtur ostendi, quod solius Dei sit secundum veritatem judicium, quia corda hominum nosse et mentis secreta dignoscere, solius est Dei. Sunt enim quædam quæ committuntur, opere quidem malo, animo autem non malo : ut si quis, verbi causa, hominem non voluntate occiderit. Alia vero fiunt opere bono, sed animo non bono : ut si quis misericordiæ opus, non pro Dei mandato, sed ut laudetur ab hominibus, faciat. Hoc tamen non est sic accipiendum, quasi judicia hominum non sint justa et vera, sed quod non sunt tam universaliter vera et justa, nec adeo certa, maxime subtracta illuminatione divina.
1.en: This the Apostle then makes plain. [[2:2|For we know|Scimus enim]] by natural reason or supernatural enlightening, [[2:2|that the judgment of God is, according to truth|quoniam judicium Dei est secundum veritatem]], that is, according to justice, by which he renders to each what he deserves; that is, we know that the judgment of God is just, [[2:2|against them|in eos]], [[2:2|that do such things|qui talia agunt]], that is, who rashly judge one another, as has just been said. For such men God rejects. On which Origen says: This seems to be shown here, that judgment according to truth belongs to God alone, because to know the hearts of men and discern the secrets of the mind belongs to God alone. For some things are committed with an evil deed but not an evil mind: as if someone, for example, killed a man without willing it. Others are done with a good deed but not a good mind: as if someone does a work of mercy, not for God's command, but to be praised by men. This, however, is not to be taken as though the judgments of men were not just and true, but that they are not so universally true and just, nor so certain, above all when divine enlightening is withdrawn.

1.t: Existimas autem hoc, o homo omnis, qui judicas inordinate eos qui talia agunt, id est, præmemorata peccata committunt, et facis ea quæ in aliis judicas, quia tu effugies judicium Dei, hoc est, damnationis sententiam et justa tormenta? quasi dicat : Noli hoc æstimare. Loquitur Apostolus interrogative.
1.en: [[2:3|And thinkest thou this, O man, that judgest|Existimas autem hoc, o homo omnis, qui judicas]] inordinately [[2:3|them who do such things|eos qui talia agunt]], that is, commit the sins mentioned before, [[2:3|and dost the same|et facis ea]] which you judge in others, [[2:3|that thou shalt escape the judgment of God?|quia tu effugies judicium Dei?]], that is, the sentence of damnation and just torments? As if he were saying: Do not think so. The Apostle speaks by way of a question.

1.t: An divitias bonitatis ejus, id est plenitudinem seu abundantiam pietatis divinæ, et patientiæ, qua non statim ulciscitur illatam sibi injuriam, et longanimitatis, qua diu iniquorum conversionem exspectat, ut indulgentiam consequantur : juxta illud Prophetæ, Propterea exspectat Dominus, ut misereatur vestri. Non enim vult mortem peccatoris, sed ut converta tur et vivat. Patientia autem quum sit virtus moralis passionem tristitiæ ordinans, non proprie competit Deo nisi per similitudinem operis. An ergo ista contemnis? quasi dicat : Mirum est si tantam pietatem et gratiam Dei non pensas neque honoras. Hanc contemnit, qui ex pia dilatione ultionis divinæ pejoratur, peccando securius, et concessa pœnitentiæ tempora expendendo in actibus pravis : quemadmodum scriptum est de ingrato ac impio, Dedit illi Deus locum pœnitentiæ, et ille abutitur eo in superbiam. Ignoras quoniam benignitas Dei ad pœnitentiam te adducit? id est, hoc merito ignorare non debes, quod misericordia Dei te patienter ac longanimiter sustinendo, quantum in se est instigat et ducit te ad pœnitentiam peragendam. Per inspirationem enim angelicam ac divinum instinctum admonentur iniqui converti ad Dominum. Unde Sapiens, Misereris (in quit) omnium, Domine, et dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam.
1.en: [[2:4|Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness|An divitias bonitatis ejus]], that is, the fulness or abundance of the divine loving-kindness, [[2:4|and patience|et patientiæ]], by which he does not straightway avenge the injury done him, [[2:4|and longsuffering|et longanimitatis]], by which he waits long for the conversion of the wicked, that they may obtain pardon: according to that of the Prophet, [[Is 30:18|the Lord waiteth that he may have mercy on you|exspectat Dominus, ut misereatur vestri]]. For he wills not the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live[[Ezech 33:11||]]. Now patience, since it is a moral virtue ordering the passion of sadness, does not properly belong to God except by likeness of working. Do you then *despise* these things? As if he were saying: it is strange if you do not weigh or honour such great loving-kindness and grace of God. He despises it who grows worse from the loving delay of divine vengeance, sinning more securely, and spending the times granted for penance in wicked acts: as it is written of the ungrateful and wicked man, [[Job 24:23|God hath given him place for penance, and he abuseth it unto pride|Dedit illi Deus locum pœnitentiæ, et ille abutitur eo in superbiam]]. [[2:4|Knowest thou not that the benignity of God leadeth thee to penance?|Ignoras quoniam benignitas Dei ad pœnitentiam te adducit?]] That is, you rightly ought not to be ignorant of this, that the mercy of God, by bearing with you patiently and long, as far as lies in it, urges and leads you to do penance[[2 Pet 3:9||]]. For by angelic inspiration and divine prompting the wicked are admonished to be converted to the Lord. Hence the Wise Man: [[Wis 11:24|thou hast mercy upon all|Misereris (in quit) omnium, Domine]] (he says), O Lord, [[Wis 11:24|and overlookest the sins of men for the sake of repentance|et dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam]].

1.t: Deinde ostendit Apostolus quid homo meretur incidere, non attendendo bonitatem longanimitatis ac patientiæ Dei, qui pie præstolatur pœnitentiam nostram. Secundum duritiam autem tuam, per obstinationem ac pertinaciam qua divinæ inspirationi resistis, nec verbo Dei mentem tuam aperis, et impœnitens cor tuum, quod de pristinis malis non dolet, nec futura vitare molitur, thesaurizas, id est multiplicas, tibi iram, id est districtam vindictam exercendam, in die iræ et revelationis justi judicii Dei, id est in die novissimo, in quo Deus maxime iratus videbitur, et secreta producet in lucem. Tunc enim revelabit abscondita tenebrarum, et manifestabit consilia cordium. Hinc scriptum est: Cor durum male habebit in novissimo. Et de peccatore indurato Dominus ait per Prophetam: Scio, quia durus es tu, et nervus ferreus cervix tua, et frons tua ærea.
1.en: Then the Apostle shows what a man deserves to fall into by not heeding the goodness of God's longsuffering and patience, who lovingly waits for our penance. [[2:5|But according to thy hardness|Secundum duritiam autem tuam]], through the obstinacy and stubbornness by which you resist divine inspiration and do not open your mind to the word of God, [[2:5|and impenitent heart|et impœnitens cor tuum]], which does not grieve for past evils nor strive to avoid future ones, [[2:5|thou treasurest up|thesaurizas]], that is, multiply, [[2:5|to thyself wrath|tibi iram]], that is, strict vengeance to be exercised, [[2:5|against the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God|in die iræ et revelationis justi judicii Dei]], that is, on the last day, on which God will appear most angry, and will bring secrets to light. For then he [[1 Cor 4:5|will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts|revelabit abscondita tenebrarum, et manifestabit consilia cordium]]. Hence it is written: [[Ecclus 3:27|A hard heart shall fear evil at the last|Cor durum male habebit in novissimo]] [*male habebit*, "shall fare ill"]. And of the hardened sinner the Lord says through the Prophet: [[Is 48:4|I knew that thou art stubborn, and thy neck is as an iron sinew, and thy forehead as brass|Scio, quia durus es tu, et nervus ferreus cervix tua, et frons tua ærea]].

1.t: Qui reddet unicuique secundum opera ejus: juxta illud Apocalypsis: Ecce venio cito, et merces mea mecum est, dare unicuique secundum opera sua. Hoc novi et veteris Testamenti Scriptura concorditer clamat. Unde in Ecclesiaste scribitur: Cuncta quæ fiunt adducet Deus in judicium pro omni errato, sive bonum, sive malum. Et Jeremias propheta: Domine, cujus oculi aperti sunt super omnes filios Adam, ut reddas unicuique secundum vias suas. In his autem atque similibus locis Scripturæ, per vias seu opera, intelligendi sunt quicumque actus humani, tam interiores quam exteriores, videlicet cogitatio, affectio, locutio, operatio.
1.en: [[2:6|Who will render to every man according to his works|Qui reddet unicuique secundum opera ejus]]: according to that of the Apocalypse, [[Apoc 22:12|Behold, I come quickly: and my reward is with me, to render to every, man according to his works|Ecce venio cito, et merces mea mecum est, dare unicuique secundum opera sua]]. This the Scripture of the New and the Old Testament cries out with one voice. Hence it is written in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 12:14|And all things that are done, God will bring into judgment for every error, whether it be good or evil|Cuncta quæ fiunt adducet Deus in judicium pro omni errato, sive bonum, sive malum]]. And Jeremias the prophet: Lord, [[Jer 32:19|whose eyes are open upon all the ways of the children of Adam, to render unto every one according to his ways|cujus oculi aperti sunt super omnes filios Adam, ut reddas unicuique secundum vias suas]]. In these and like places of Scripture, by ways or works are to be understood any human acts whatever, inward as well as outward, namely thought, affection, speech and deed.

1.t: Consequenter ostenditur in specie, quod dicebatur in genere. His quidem qui secundum patientiam boni operis, gloriam et honorem. Sic legenda est littera: Deus reddet singulis secundum opera sua: his quidem qui sunt boni operis: id est bonæ vitæ, secundum patientiam Dei, qui eorum conversionem longanimiter expectavit, et ita bene usi sunt patientia Dei, reddet pro præmio gloriam, id est beatitudinem sive lætitiam, vel claram cum laude notitiam, clarificando eos in cordibus aliorum, et honorem, id est reverentiæ exhibitionem in signum virtutis ipsorum: nam et Deus honorabit eos, constituendo eos secum in regno cælorum; et incorruptionem, id est immortalitatem, impassibilitatem, atque perpetuam securitatem: his, inquam, quærentibus vitam æternam, id est referentibus cuncta quæ agunt, ad ultimum finem seu veram felicitatem, quæ est vita æterna, non ad temporale commodum aut laudem humanam. Unde ait Salvator: Primum quærite regnum Dei; et Apostolus. Quæ sursum sunt quærite. Hoc modo exponitur littera ista communiter. — Videtur quoque sic posse exponi: His qui secundum patientiam boni operis sunt, id est, qui opera bona patienter egerunt, et per patientiam custodierunt, dabit gloriam et honorem. Propter quod dicit Salvator: In patientia vestra possidebitis animas vestras. Vel sic: His qui secundum patientiam ambulaverunt, id est, patienter conversati sunt, retribuet Deus boni operis, id est pro bono opere, gloriam et honorem, tanquam condignam mercedem.
1.en: Next what was said in general is shown in particular. [[2:7|To them indeed who, according to patience in good work, seek glory and honour|His quidem qui secundum patientiam boni operis, gloriam et honorem]]. The text is to be read thus: God will render to each according to his works: *to them indeed* who are *of good work*, that is, of good life, *according to the patience* of God, who waited long for their conversion, and so they have used God's patience well, he will render as reward *glory*, that is, beatitude or gladness, or a bright knowledge joined with praise, making them glorious in the hearts of others, *and honour*, that is, the showing of reverence as a sign of their virtue: for God too will honour them, setting them with himself in the kingdom of heaven; [[2:7|and incorruption|et incorruptionem]], that is, immortality, impassibility and perpetual security: to them, I say, *who seek* [[2:7|eternal life|vitam æternam]], that is, who refer all they do to the last end, or true happiness, which is eternal life, not to temporal advantage or human praise. Hence the Saviour says: [[Matt 6:33|Seek ye therefore first the kingdom of God|Primum quærite regnum Dei]]; and the Apostle, [[Col 3:1|seek the things that are above|Quæ sursum sunt quærite]]. In this way the text is commonly expounded. It seems it can also be expounded thus: To those who are according to the patience of good work, that is, who have done good works patiently and kept them by patience, he will give glory and honour. For which reason the Saviour says: [[Luke 21:19|In your patience you shall possess your souls|In patientia vestra possidebitis animas vestras]]. Or thus: to those who have walked according to patience, that is, have lived patiently, God will repay, for good work, that is, in return for good work, glory and honour, as a worthy reward.

1.t: His autem qui sunt ex contentione, id est, insimul litigant et pacis jura violant, vel Deo resistere satagunt, et qui non acquiescunt veritati, id est justitiæ seu sanæ doctrinæ qua admonentur converti ad Deum, credunt autem iniquitati, id est vanis erroribus ac falsis dogmatibus: quo contra dicit Apostolus ad Hebræos, Doctrinis variis et peregrinis nolite abduci. His itaque superveniet ira, id est divina ultio, et indignatio, id est detestatio qua Judex æternus eos contemnet, tribulatio corporis, et angustia mentis: venient, inquam, hæc, in omnem animam hominis operantis malum, nisi pœniteat (nam et corporis pœna redundat in animam, et converso), Judæi primum, id est præcipue, quoniam propter legem divinam ei traditam gravius peccavit, et fortius punietur, et Græci. Si per Græcos intelligatur gens illa specialis, tunc Græcus post Judæum exprimitur, quia præ ceteris gentibus magis peccavit atque punitus est, eo quod in naturali philosophia et subtilitate ingenii præfulgebat. Ubi enim majus donum scientiæ, ibi prævaricator graviori subjacet culpæ et pœnæ. Si vero per Græcum intelligantur gentiles communiter, tunc post Judæum ponitur Græcus, quoniam minus peccavit, loquendo in genere, et ceteris paribus.
1.en: [[2:8|But to them that are contentious|His autem qui sunt ex contentione]], that is, who quarrel among themselves and break the laws of peace, or busy themselves in resisting God, [[2:8|and who obey not the truth|et qui non acquiescunt veritati]], that is, justice, or the sound teaching by which they are admonished to be converted to God, [[2:8|but give credit to iniquity|credunt autem iniquitati]], that is, to vain errors and false dogmas: against which the Apostle says to the Hebrews, [[Heb 13:9|Be not led away with various and strange doctrines|Doctrinis variis et peregrinis nolite abduci]]. On these, then, will come [[2:8|wrath|ira]], that is, divine vengeance, [[2:8|and indignation|et indignatio]], that is, the abhorrence with which the eternal Judge will despise them, [[2:9|Tribulation|tribulatio]] of body, [[2:9|and anguish|et angustia]] of mind: these, I say, will come [[2:9|upon every soul of man that worketh evil|in omnem animam hominis operantis malum]], unless he repent (for the punishment of the body also overflows into the soul, and conversely), [[2:9|of the Jew first|Judæi primum]], that is, chiefly, since because of the divine law given him he sinned more gravely and will be punished more heavily, [[2:9|and also of the Greek|et Græci]]. If by Greeks is understood that particular nation, then the Greek is named after the Jew because more than the other nations he sinned and was punished, since he shone in natural philosophy and subtlety of wit. For where the gift of knowledge is greater, there the transgressor is subject to a heavier fault and punishment. But if by the Greek are understood the Gentiles in common, then the Greek is placed after the Jew because he sinned less, speaking in general and other things being equal.

1.t: His verbis Apostoli consonat illud Proverbiorum quod ex persona æternæ Sapientiæ dicitur: Quia vocavi et renuistis, et extendi manum meam, et non fuit qui aspiceret, et despexistis omne consilium meum, et increpationes meas neglexistis, ego[…] quoque in interitu vestro ridebo, quum irruerit repentina calamitas, et interitus quasi tempestas ingruerit, quando venerit super vos tribulatio et angustia. Hoc loco Apostolus contentiosos redarguit. Unde de et Jacobus apostolus dicit : Si zelum amarum habetis, et contentiones sunt inter vos, nolite gloriari, et mendaces esse adversus veritatem. Denique tanta est culpa contentionis, ut propter ipsam corporalis exercitatio reprobetur, dicente Domino per Prophetam : Ecce ad lites et contentiones jejunatis : numquid tale est jejunium quod elegi?
1.en: With these words of the Apostle agrees that of Proverbs, which is said in the person of the eternal Wisdom: [[Prov 1:24|Because I called, and you refused: I stretched out my hand, and there was none that regarded|Quia vocavi et renuistis, et extendi manum meam, et non fuit qui aspiceret]], [[Prov 1:25|You have despised all my counsel, and have neglected my reprehensions|despexistis omne consilium meum, et increpationes meas neglexistis]], [[Prov 1:26|I also will laugh in your destruction|ego quoque in interitu vestro ridebo]], [[Prov 1:27|When sudden calamity shall fall on you, and destruction, as a tempest, shall be at hand: when tribulation and distress shall come upon you|quum irruerit repentina calamitas, et interitus quasi tempestas ingruerit, quando venerit super vos tribulatio et angustia]]. In this place the Apostle rebukes the contentious. Hence James the apostle too says: [[Jas 3:14|But if you have bitter zeal, and there be contention in your hearts: glory not and be not liars against the truth|Si zelum amarum habetis, et contentiones sunt inter vos, nolite gloriari, et mendaces esse adversus veritatem]]. Lastly, so great is the fault of contention that because of it even bodily discipline is rejected, as the Lord says through the Prophet: [[Is 58:4|Behold you fast for debates and strife|Ecce ad lites et contentiones jejunatis]]: [[Is 58:5|Is this such a fast as I have chosen|numquid tale est jejunium quod elegi?]]?

1.t: Gloria autem et honor, de quibus jam dictum est, et pax, id est tranquillitas mentis, seu securitas ab impugnatione hostili, dabuntur pro præmio omni operanti bonum ex caritate, Judæo primum, id est præcipue : quia in genere plus aliis meruerunt Judæi ad Christum conversi, videlicet sancti Apostoli, ac primitiva Ecclesia; et Græco, id est gentilibus.
1.en: [[2:10|But glory and honour|Gloria autem et honor]], of which we have already spoken, [[2:10|and peace|et pax]], that is, tranquillity of mind, or security from the enemy's attack, will be given as a reward [[2:10|to every one that worketh good|omni operanti bonum]] out of charity, [[2:10|to the Jew first|Judæo primum]], that is, chiefly: because in general the Jews converted to Christ, namely the holy Apostles and the early Church, merited more than others; [[2:10|and also to the Greek|et Græco]], that is, to the Gentiles.

1.t: Non est enim acceptio personarum apud Deum : id est, Deus in judicando non attendit personam, et ea quæ non habent rationem meriti sive demeriti, sed sola opera pensat, et unumquemque secundum merita sua judicat. Propter quod asserebat Petrus : In veritate comperi quoniam non est personarum acceptor Deus; sed in omni gente, qui timet Deum et operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi. Et per Prophetam Dominus loquitur : Unumquemque juxta vias suas judicabo. Ad hanc perfectionem hortatur nos sermo divinus, per Moysen dicens : Juste judicabis, nec consideres personam pauperis, neque honores vultum potentis.
1.en: [[2:11|For there is no respect of persons with God|Non est enim acceptio personarum apud Deum]]: that is, God in judging does not regard the person, and those things which have no ground of merit or demerit, but weighs the works alone, and judges each according to his merits. For which reason Peter declared: [[Acts 10:34|in very deed I perceive that God is not a respecter of persons|In veritate comperi quoniam non est personarum acceptor Deus]]; [[Acts 10:35|But in every nation, he that feareth him and worketh justice is acceptable to him|sed in omni gente, qui timet Deum et operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi]]. And through the Prophet the Lord says: [[Ezech 33:20|I will judge every one of you according to his ways|Unumquemque juxta vias suas judicabo]]. To this perfection the divine word exhorts us, saying through Moses: [[Lev 19:15|Respect not the person of the poor: nor honour the countenance of the mighty|nec consideres personam pauperis, neque honores vultum potentis]] [Denis begins, "Thou shalt judge justly"].

1.t: Porro, quod apud Deum non sit personarum acceptio, sed justum judicium, probat. Quicumque enim sine lege scripta atque Mosaica peccaverunt, videlicet non habendo legem, id est gentiles qui peccatum commiserunt, non quia legem scriptam transgressi sunt, quia nec eam habuerunt, sine lege peribunt, id est, non propter hujus legis prævaricationem damnabuntur, sed propter hoc quod legem naturalem non servaverunt cum fide Salvatoris saltem implicita, ut plenius ostendetur. Quum autem dicat Ambrosius, Peccatum est prævaricatio legis divinæ, quæri potest, quomodo aliquis peccare valeat sine lege. Et respondendum, quod in definitione Ambrosii, per legem divinam intelligitur quælibet lex data a Deo, a quo constat naturalem legem fluxisse, datamque esse. Et quicumque in lege scripta peccaverunt, eam non observando, sicut Judæi, per legem, id est ex ipsa lege scripta, vel propter legis transgressionem, judicabuntur judicio reprobationis. Unde Christus aiebat Judæis : Est qui accusat vos Moyses, in quo vos speratis.
1.en: Further, he proves that with God there is no respect of persons, but just judgment. [[2:12|For whosoever have sinned without the law|Quicumque enim sine lege peccaverunt]], the written law of Moses, namely by not having the law, that is, the Gentiles who committed sin, not because they transgressed the written law, since they did not have it, [[2:12|shall perish without the law|sine lege peribunt]], that is, they will be damned not for breaking this law, but because they did not keep the natural law with at least an implicit faith in the Saviour, as will be shown more fully. Now since Ambrose says, *Sin is the breaking of the divine law*, it may be asked how anyone can sin without the law. The answer is that in Ambrose's definition by divine law is understood any law given by God, from whom it is certain the natural law flowed and was given. [[2:12|and whosoever have sinned in the law|Et quicumque in lege scripta peccaverunt]], the written law, by not keeping it, as the Jews, [[2:12|shall be judged by the law|per legem judicabuntur]], that is, from the written law itself, or for transgressing the law, with the judgment of reprobation. Hence Christ said to the Jews: [[John 5:45|There is one that accuseth you, Moses, in whom you trust|Est qui accusat vos Moyses, in quo vos speratis]].

1.t: Non enim auditores legis divinitus datæ, justi sunt apud Deum, nisi obediant legi : ideo subditur, sed factores legis, id est, qui legis mandata adimplent, justificabuntur, id est, justi erunt ac reputabuntur apud Deum. Nam et fides sine operibus mortua est. Et in Evangelio Christus testatur : Omnis qui audit verba hæc, et non facit ea, assimilabitur viro stulto qui ædificavit domum suam supra arenam; et alibi, Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud. Ipsa ergo impletio legis per gratiam, ex qua procedit impletio, justificat hominem, estque justificatio ejus.
1.en: [[2:13|For not the hearers of the law|Non enim auditores legis]] given by God [[2:13|are just before God|justi sunt apud Deum]], unless they obey the law: therefore it is added, [[2:13|but the doers of the law|sed factores legis]], that is, those who fulfil the commandments of the law, [[2:13|shall be justified|justificabuntur]], that is, will be, and be accounted, just before God. For [[Jas 2:20|faith without works is dead|fides sine operibus mortua est]]. And in the Gospel Christ testifies: [[Matt 7:26|And every one that heareth these my words and doth them not, shall be like a foolish man that built his house upon the sand|Omnis qui audit verba hæc, et non facit ea, assimilabitur viro stulto qui ædificavit domum suam supra arenam]]; and elsewhere, [[Luke 11:28|blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it|Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud]]. The very fulfilling of the law, then, through grace, from which the fulfilling proceeds, justifies a man, and is his justification.

1.t: Denique, quod ipsa observatio legis justificet, elucescit ex hoc : Quum enim gentes, id est gentiles, quæ legem scriptam seu Moysis non habent, quia non tenebantur ad eam, naturaliter, id est ex naturalis rationis dictamine, adjuti tamen lumine gratiæ, sine qua nemo unquam salvatus est : non enim ex puris naturalibus quisquam salvatur, quum salus nostra sit supernaturalis felicitas, scilicet visio per speciem, ad quam sine fide, caritate et gratia Dei nullus viator pertingit; ea quæ legis sunt faciunt, id est, legem scriptam observant, quantum ad præcepta moralia Decalogi, quæ sunt de dictamine rationis naturalis; ejusmo di gentes legem Mosaicam non habentes, ipsi sibi sunt lex, id est, propria ratio est eis pro lege; qui ostendunt, bene vivendo, opus legis, quod a lege scripta præcipitur fieri aut vitari, scriptum in cordibus suis, id est intellectu naturali impressum : ita quod ratio dictat eis quod dictat lex scripta. Dum enim non faciunt alteri quod sibi nolunt fieri, quod utique naturalis ratio dictat, implent ea quæ jubet lex scripta. Nam et secundum Apostolum, Qui diligit proximum, legem implevit.
1.en: Lastly, that the very keeping of the law justifies is made clear from this: [[2:14|For when the Gentiles|Quum enim gentes]], that is, the heathen, [[2:14|who have not the law|quæ legem non habent]], the written law of Moses, since they were not bound to it, [[2:14|do by nature|naturaliter]], that is, by the dictate of natural reason, helped however by the light of grace, without which no one has ever been saved (for no one is saved from pure nature alone, since our salvation is a supernatural happiness, namely vision by sight, which no wayfarer reaches without faith, charity and the grace of God), [[2:14|those things that are of the law|ea quæ legis sunt faciunt]], that is, keep the written law as to the moral precepts of the Decalogue, which are of the dictate of natural reason; [[2:14|these, having not the law|ejusmodi … legem … non habentes]], Gentiles of this kind not having the law of Moses, [[2:14|are a law to themselves|ipsi sibi sunt lex]], that is, their own reason is law for them; [[2:15|Who shew the work of the law|qui ostendunt, bene vivendo, opus legis]] by living well, the work which the written law commands to be done or avoided, [[2:15|written in their hearts|scriptum in cordibus suis]], that is, impressed on the natural understanding: so that reason dictates to them what the written law dictates. For when they do not do to another what they would not have done to themselves[[Tob 4:16||]][[Matt 7:12||]], which natural reason surely dictates, they fulfil what the written law commands. For according to the Apostle too, [[Rom 13:8|he that loveth his neighbour hath fulfilled the law|Qui diligit proximum, legem implevit]].

1.t: Hi ergo qui naturaliter agunt ea quæ legis sunt, sibi sunt lex : quod declarat Apostolus per effectum, videlicet per conscientiæ testimonium. Subditur enim, testimonium boni vel mali reddente illis conscientia ipsorum, quæ ex naturali judicio rationis reprobat malum, et approbat bonum : recalcitrat enim quodammodo operi vitioso, consentitque actui virtuoso; et inter se invicem cogitationum accusantium, aut etiam defendentium. More Græcorum ponit genitivum pro ablativo, ut sit sensus : Cogitationibus se invicem accusantibus, id est perversis cogitationibus quæ malos accusant, aut etiam defendentibus, id est cogitationibus bonis quæ bonos excusant atque defendunt : his, inquam, cogitationibus testimonium damnationis vel salutis reddentibus illis, id est prædictis gentilibus. Istæ cogitationes accusantes ac defendentes, hoc est malæ ac bonæ, examinantur, dijudicantur et declarantur coram naturali judicatorio hominis, quasi coram judice, per prima agibilium principia naturaliter inserta et cognita, sicut est illud : Quod tibi vis fieri, fac alteri.
