4.title_en: Explanation of the fourth chapter: What shall we say then that Abraham hath found?

paras.t: Declarata insufficientia legis ad salutem per rationem, jam idem ostendit per exemplum, et ait : Quid ergo dicemus, id est, si juxta præinducta circumcisio et præputium, seu Judæus et gentilis, communiter atque æqualiter justificantur per fidem, quid tunc dicemus invenisse Abraham patrem nostrum secundum carnem, id est secundum carnis originem, a quo ego Paulus et ceteri Israelitæ secundum carnalem propagationem descendimus ? Vel, Secundum carnem, id est ex operibus legis carnalibus, scilicet circumcisione et sacrificiis. Quasi dicat : Ad quid profuit ei observantia carnalium operum legis, videlicet impletio cærimonialium præceptorum ? Quid autem ad hoc responderi oporteat, ex sequentibus innotescit.
paras.en: Having shown by reason that the law is insufficient for salvation, he now shows the same by an example, and says: [[4:1|What shall we say then|Quid ergo dicemus]], that is, if, according to what has been said, circumcision and uncircumcision, or Jew and Gentile, are justified alike and equally by faith, what shall we say then [[4:1|that Abraham hath found, who is our father according to the flesh?|invenisse Abraham patrem nostrum secundum carnem]], that is, according to fleshly descent, from whom I Paul and the other Israelites are descended by carnal propagation? Or, *according to the flesh*, that is, from the carnal works of the law, namely circumcision and sacrifices. As if he were saying: what did the keeping of the carnal works of the law, namely the fulfilling of the ceremonial precepts, profit him? What must be answered to this is made known from what follows.

paras.t: Respondendum est enim, quod non sit perfecte et vere justificatus ex operibus legis. Si enim Abraham ex operibus legis prædictis carnalibus justificatus est justitia vera ac meritoria, habet gloriam, id est veram beatitudinem pro mercede, sed non habet eam apud Deum, hoc est a Deo et coram eo, quoniam propria virtute, non gratia Dei, justificatus esset. Et quia hoc consequens impossibile est, ergo et illud ex quo infertur, videlicet quod Abraham justificatus sit ex operibus legis. Vel sic, et melius : Si Abraham ex operibus legis justificatus est, habet gloriam, id est, dignus est laude ac præmio pro sua justitia, sed non apud Deum, quia justitia talis non fecit eum dignum vita æterna. Ex parte enim operis operati, non erant præfata opera legis meritoria, nec ipsa lex gratiam contulit per quam justificarentur observatores ipsius, sicut lex nova, quæ gratiam confert propter sacramenta quæ includit : quæ sunt signa et causa gratiæ justificantis. Operantur quippe quod significant : quod sacramentis veteris Testamenti non competit.
paras.en: For the answer is that he was not perfectly and truly justified by the works of the law. [[4:2|For if Abraham were justified by works|Si enim Abraham ex operibus justificatus est]] of the law spoken of, the carnal ones, with true and meritorious justice, [[4:2|he hath whereof to glory|habet gloriam]], that is, true beatitude as reward, [[4:2|but not before God|sed non apud Deum]], that is, from God and in his sight, since he would have been justified by his own power, not by the grace of God. And since this consequence is impossible, so also is that from which it is inferred, namely that Abraham was justified by the works of the law. Or thus, and better: if Abraham was justified by the works of the law, he has glory, that is, he is worthy of praise and reward for his justice, but not before God, because such justice did not make him worthy of eternal life. For on the side of the work done [*ex opere operato*], the works of the law spoken of were not meritorious, nor did the law itself confer grace by which those who kept it might be justified, as the new law does, which confers grace through the sacraments it contains: which are signs and causes of justifying grace. For they bring about what they signify: which does not belong to the sacraments of the Old Testament.

paras.t: Deinde probat auctoritate Scripturæ, quod Abraham justificatus est per fidem, non per opera legis. Quid enim Scriptura dicit? Credidit Abraham Deo promittenti sibi per angelum propagationem innumerabilium filiorum instar stellarum ; et alibi, In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes : […] est, merito fidei justus justificatus est coram Deo, et dignus effectus est vita æterna per actum interiorem fidei suæ, secundum quod actus ille etiam ex caritate imperative processit. Ei autem qui operatur, merces non imputatur secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum. Ei vero qui non operatur, credenti autem in eum qui justificat impium, reputatur fides ejus ad justitiam secundum propositum gratiæ Dei. Hucusque littera cohæret et condependet : quæ difficultatibus plena est.
paras.en: Next he proves by the authority of Scripture that Abraham was justified by faith, not by the works of the law. [[4:3|For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God|Quid enim Scriptura dicit? Credidit Abraham Deo]], who promised him through an angel the propagation of innumerable children like the stars[[Gen 15:6||]]; and elsewhere, [[Gen 22:18|in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes]]: […] [a line is lost here in the transcription] that is, by the merit of faith the just man was justified before God, and was made worthy of eternal life by the inward act of his faith, inasmuch as that act also proceeded by command from charity. [[4:4|Now to him that worketh, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt|Ei autem qui operatur, merces non imputatur secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum]]. [[4:5|But to him that worketh not, yet believeth in him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is reputed to justice, according to the purpose of the grace of God|Ei vero qui non operatur, credenti autem in eum qui justificat impium, reputatur fides ejus ad justitiam secundum propositum gratiæ Dei]]. Up to here the text hangs together and depends on itself: and it is full of difficulties.

paras.t: Porro, secundum B. Ambrosium, introducenda, continuanda, et exponenda est ita : Jam dixit Apostolus Abraham non ex operibus, sed ex fide justificatum. Ex quo sequi videtur, fidem sine operibus sufficere ad salutem. Contra quod tamen Dominus ait : Non omnis qui dicit mihi, Domine, Domine, intrabit in regnum cœlorum, sed qui facit voluntatem Patris mei ; et iterum, Si vis, inquit, ingredi ad vitam, serva mandata. Jacobus quoque apostolus testatur : Quid proderit, si quis dicat fidem se habere, opera autem ipsa non habeat? Fides si non habet opera, mortua est in se ipsa. Hinc etiam paulo ante dixit Apostolus : Non auditores legis, sed factores legis justificabuntur. — Hanc objectionem solvit Apostolus, dicens : Ei autem qui operatur, id est, qui tempus et opportunitatem habet operandi, merces non imputatur, id est, præmium non confertur, secundum gratiam fidei tantum, id est, non gratis sine operibus præmium consequitur : in tali enim fides sine operibus mortua est ; sed secundum debitum operationis, ad quam ex divino mandato tenetur, merces ei imputatur ac datur. Nam sine operibus salvari non potest. Quod si operari neglexerit, damnabitur. Ei vero qui non operatur, id est, opportunitatem seu tempus et locum operandi non habet, credenti autem in eum qui justificat impium, hoc est in Christum, qui peccatori gratis ignoscit, gratiamque infundit, ante cujus infusionem peccator veniam promereri non potest de condigno, reputatur fides ejus, id est actus fidei suæ interior sine opere exteriore, ad justitiam, ita quod sufficit ei ad salutem, ut in latrone : bona enim voluntas seu præparatio animi ad opus, reputatur ei pro opere ; secundum propositum gratiæ Dei, id est secundum voluntatem miserationis divinæ, vel secundum ordinem gratiæ Dei nobis oblatæ, qui taliter voluit nos salvare. In quo patet virtus ac sufficientia fidei. Per hoc vero quod ait, Credenti in eum, certum est Apostolum loqui de fide formata, quæ per dilectionem fertur in Deum, et operatur si opportunitas adsit. Hæc expositio procedit de operibus ipsam fidem sequentibus, atque ex ea nascentibus.
paras.en: Further, according to Blessed Ambrose, it is to be introduced, connected and expounded thus. The Apostle has just said that Abraham was justified not by works but by faith. From which it seems to follow that faith without works suffices for salvation. Against which, however, the Lord says: [[Matt 7:21|Not every one that saith to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven|Non omnis qui dicit mihi, Domine, Domine, intrabit in regnum cœlorum]], [[Matt 7:21|but he that doth the will of my Father|sed qui facit voluntatem Patris mei]]; and again, [[Matt 19:17|if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments|Si vis, inquit, ingredi ad vitam, serva mandata]] (he says). James the apostle also testifies: [[Jas 2:14|What shall it profit, my brethren, if a man say he hath faith, but hath not works?|Quid proderit, si quis dicat fidem se habere, opera autem ipsa non habeat?]] [[Jas 2:17|if it have not works, is dead in itself|Fides si non habet opera, mortua est in se ipsa]]. Hence also a little before the Apostle said: [[Rom 2:13|For not the hearers of the law are just before God: but the doers of the law shall be justified|Non auditores legis, sed factores legis justificabuntur]]. This objection the Apostle resolves, saying: [[4:4|Now to him that worketh|Ei autem qui operatur]], that is, who has time and opportunity to work, [[4:4|the reward is not reckoned|merces non imputatur]], that is, the prize is not conferred, [[4:4|according to grace|secundum gratiam]] of faith alone, that is, he does not obtain the reward freely without works: for in such a man [[Jas 2:20|faith without works is dead|fides sine operibus mortua est]]; [[4:4|but according to debt|sed secundum debitum]] of working, to which he is bound by divine command, the reward is reckoned and given him. For without works he cannot be saved: and if he neglects to work he will be damned. [[4:5|But to him that worketh not|Ei vero qui non operatur]], that is, has not the opportunity, or time and place, to work, [[4:5|yet believeth in him that justifieth the ungodly|credenti autem in eum qui justificat impium]], that is, in Christ, who freely pardons the sinner and pours in grace, before whose infusion the sinner cannot merit pardon condignly [by a strict title of merit], [[4:5|his faith is reputed|reputatur fides ejus]], that is, the inward act of his faith without the outward work, [[4:5|to justice|ad justitiam]], so that it suffices him for salvation, as in the thief: for the good will, or the mind's readiness for the work, is reckoned to him for the work; [[4:5|according to the purpose of the grace of God|secundum propositum gratiæ Dei]], that is, according to the will of divine mercy, or according to the order of the grace of God offered to us, who willed to save us in this way. In which the power and sufficiency of faith is plain. And by saying, *believeth in him*, it is certain that the Apostle speaks of formed faith, which is borne towards God through love, and works if opportunity is there. This exposition proceeds of the works that follow faith and are born of it.

paras.t: Secundo exponitur de operibus præcedentibus fidem, contra illos qui asserebant merito præcedentium operum legis, se gratiam fidei esse adeptos. Quo dato, gratia non reputabitur secundum viam et ordinem gratiæ, sed secundum debitum meriti præcedentis. Quo concesso, gratia jam non erit gratia. Quoniam ergo hoc consequens impossibile est, constat quod gratiam fidei, seu ipsam fidem, nullus meretur. Ait ergo : Ei autem qui operatur aliqua bona ante fidem, merces non imputatur secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum, hoc est, si præmium ei datur pro bonis quæ fecit, hoc non erit gratis, sed ex debito meriti præcedentis : sicque fidem præcedent merita, quum tamen fides sit omnis meritorii actus principium, omniumque virtutum fundamentum. Ei vero qui non operatur opera legis cærimonialia atque carnalia, vel quæcumque alia ante fidem, sicut gentilis, credenti autem per fidem formatam in eum qui justificat impium, id est in Christum, reputatur fides ejus ad justitiam, secundum sensum prætactum : et hoc, secundum propositum gratiæ Dei, id est secundum gratuitum atque benignum Dei decretum, qui ita decrevit ut onere legis ablato, homines fide justificentur ac salventur.
paras.en: Secondly it is expounded of the works that go before faith, against those who asserted that they had obtained the grace of faith by the merit of works of the law going before. Granting which, grace would not be reckoned according to the way and order of grace, but according to the debt of preceding merit. And granting this, grace would no longer be grace. Since then this consequence is impossible, it is certain that no one merits the grace of faith, or faith itself. He says therefore: [[4:4|Now to him that worketh|Ei autem qui operatur]] some good works before faith, [[4:4|the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt|merces non imputatur secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum]], that is, if a reward is given him for the good he has done, this will not be free, but from the debt of preceding merit: and so merits would go before faith, though faith is the beginning of every meritorious act and the foundation of all the virtues. [[4:5|But to him that worketh not|Ei vero qui non operatur]] the ceremonial and carnal works of the law, or any others before faith, as the Gentile, [[4:5|yet believeth|credenti autem]] by formed faith [[4:5|in him that justifieth the ungodly|in eum qui justificat impium]], that is, in Christ, [[4:5|his faith is reputed to justice|reputatur fides ejus ad justitiam]], in the sense touched on before: and this [[4:5|according to the purpose of the grace of God|secundum propositum gratiæ Dei]], that is, according to the free and kindly decree of God, who so decreed that, the burden of the law being taken away, men should be justified and saved by faith.

paras.t: Tertio exponitur secundum quosdam, qui ex verbis Apostoli talem rationem inducunt : Illud quod conceditur alicui quemadmodum merces operanti, non conceditur ei per viam gratiæ, sed debiti ; justitia vero de qua sermo est, conceditur per viam gratiæ, sicut jam patuit quod Abraham justificatus est per fidem sine operibus legis : ergo justitia hæc non est ex operibus legis. Hæc autem expositio irresoluta videtur, et satis ambigua. Simili enim ratione posset ostendi, quod justitia novi Testamenti non esset ex operibus evangelicæ legis : quæ tamen justificant, habitumque justitiæ inducunt, vel augent sive perficiunt etiam ex parte operis operati, virtute sacramentorum Christi. Posset enim sic argui : Quod conceditur alicui sicut merces operanti, non conceditur ei per viam gratiæ, sed debiti ; sed justitia novæ legis conceditur per viam gratiæ. Quid enim habes quod non accepisti ? non ergo est ex operibus novæ legis. Denique caritas agens, et cetera virtutes per caritatem agentes, merentur gratiam ampliorem in præsenti, gloriamque in futuro, et redditur eis merces ista. Nihilo minus redditio hujus mercedis, est secundum viam gratiæ, et secundum viam debiti, secundum diversos respectus. Quum enim prima infusio gratiæ sit solum gratuita, omnia bona quæ per gratiam illam merentur, gratuite præmiantur per comparationem ad gratiam primam.
paras.en: Thirdly it is expounded according to some, who draw such an argument from the Apostle's words: what is granted to someone as a reward to one who works is not granted him by way of grace but of debt; but the justice spoken of is granted by way of grace, as it has just appeared that Abraham was justified by faith without the works of the law: therefore this justice is not from the works of the law. But this exposition seems unresolved and rather ambiguous. For by a like argument it could be shown that the justice of the New Testament is not from the works of the law of the Gospel: which nevertheless justify, and bring in the habit of justice, or increase or perfect it, even on the side of the work done, by the power of the sacraments of Christ. For one could argue thus: what is granted to someone as a reward to one who works is not granted him by way of grace but of debt; but the justice of the new law is granted by way of grace: [[1 Cor 4:7|what hast thou that thou hast not received|Quid enim habes quod non accepisti]]? therefore it is not from the works of the new law. Lastly, charity acting, and the other virtues acting through charity, merit greater grace in the present and glory in the future, and this reward is rendered them. Nevertheless the rendering of this reward is by way of grace and by way of debt, under different respects. For since the first infusion of grace is only free, all the goods merited through that grace are rewarded freely by comparison with the first grace.

paras.t: Satisfeci forsan lectori in expositione præsentis loci, sed non mihi ipsi, quia profunditatem verborum istorum intelligere non valeo, neque connexionem eorum cum præcedentibus atque sequentibus plene concipio. Consolatus tamen est me sermo, quem ex ore viri doctissimi sacræ Theologiæ professoris condigni audivi, qui dixit : In epistolis Pauli habet elephas ubi submergatur, quanto magis pulex, ut sum ego ? Unde in similibus locis comedam quantum possum ; quod autem residuum fuerit, igne comburam, sanctorum et catholicorum doctorum expositionem sequens, et ea contentus. Non enim quisquam mortalium penetrare valet profunditatem epistolarum divi Pauli apostoli.
paras.en: I have perhaps satisfied the reader in the exposition of this present place, but not myself, since I cannot understand the depth of these words, nor fully grasp their connexion with what goes before and what follows. Yet I was comforted by a saying I heard from the mouth of a most learned man, a worthy professor of sacred Theology, who said: In the epistles of Paul the elephant has where to drown; how much more the flea, such as I am? Hence in like places I will eat as much as I can, and what is left over I will burn with fire [as with the paschal lamb, Ex 12:10], following and content with the exposition of the holy and Catholic doctors. For no mortal can penetrate the depth of the epistles of the divine apostle Paul.

paras.t: Præmissa autem probat Apostolus auctoritate Psalmistæ, subjungens : Sicut et David dicit beatitudinem hominis, id est illum esse beatum, seu beatitudinem esse illius in via per spem, et in patria per speciem, cui homini Deus accepto, id est tempore gratiæ, de quo legitur, Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile ; vel, Accepto, id est acceptanter, gratis et pie ; fert, donat et ingerit justitiam, hoc est remissionem peccati, et gratiæ atque virtutum infusionem, sine operibus legalibus et humanis, quæ per se nequaquam sufficiunt ad gratiam promerendam. Nec enim potest peccator per se ipsum resurgere, sed indiget præveniri ab eo de quo legitur : Allevat Dominus omnes qui corruunt ; et iterum : Dominus erigit elisos. Nec obstat illud Augustini, Qui creavit te sine te, non justificabit te sine te. Hoc enim ideo dicitur, quia Deus requirit a nobis ut faciamus quod in nobis est, disponendo nos ad gratiam ejus.
paras.en: The Apostle proves what has been said by the authority of the Psalmist, adding: [[4:6|As David also termeth the blessedness of a man|Sicut et David dicit beatitudinem hominis]], that is, that he is blessed, or that blessedness is his, on the way by hope and in the fatherland by sight, [[4:6|to whom God|cui homini Deus]] *accepto* [Denis's text reads *Deus accepto fert justitiam*], that is, in the time of grace, of which we read, [[2 Cor 6:2|Behold, now is the acceptable time|Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile]]; or, *accepto*, that is, acceptingly, freely and lovingly, [[4:6|reputeth justice|fert justitiam]], gives and brings in justice, that is, the remission of sin and the infusion of grace and the virtues, [[4:6|without works|sine operibus]] of the law and of men, which of themselves by no means suffice to merit grace. For the sinner cannot rise again of himself, but needs to be gone before by him of whom we read: [[Ps 144:14|The Lord lifteth up all that fall|Allevat Dominus omnes qui corruunt]]; and again: [[Ps 145:8|The Lord lifteth up them that are cast down|Dominus erigit elisos]]. Nor does that saying of Augustine stand in the way: He who created you without you will not justify you without you. For this is said because God requires of us that we do what is in us, disposing ourselves for his grace.

paras.t: Deinde ponit verba Psalmistæ : Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates originales, et actuales seu personales, in Baptismo, in quo originale peccatum deletur quantum ad reatum culpæ : quia quod ante Baptismum erat culpa et pœna, post Baptismum tantum est pœna, quæ dicitur fomes peccati, quæ etiam in Baptismo per gratiam sacramenti debilitatur, sed non penitus tollitur. Peccatum autem originale formaliter unum est, materialiter plura, ratione sui effectus. Quatuor enim vulnera imprimit animæ. Propter quod ait Psalmista : Ecce enim in iniquitatibus conceptus sum. Actualia vero peccata, per cordis contritionem dimittuntur quantum ad culpam. Et quorum tecta sunt peccata, hoc est ab oculis Dei absconditа, ita quod non videantur nec imputat ea, sed avertit faciem suam ab eis, ac si nunquam fuissent. Ideo sequitur : Beatus vir cui non imputavit nec imputat Dominus peccatum, sed prorsus ignoscit, sicut per Isaiam promisit : Delebo ut nubem iniquitates tuas, et quasi caliginem peccata tua.
paras.en: Then he gives the words of the Psalmist: [[4:7|Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven|Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates]], original and actual or personal, in Baptism, in which original sin is blotted out as to the guilt of fault: since what before Baptism was fault and punishment, after Baptism is punishment only, which is called the tinder of sin [*fomes*], which is also weakened in Baptism by the grace of the sacrament, but not wholly taken away. Original sin is formally one, materially many, by reason of its effect: for it imprints four wounds on the soul. For which reason the Psalmist says: [[Ps 50:7|For behold I was conceived in iniquities|Ecce enim in iniquitatibus conceptus sum]]. And actual sins are forgiven as to their guilt by contrition of heart. [[4:7|and whose sins are covered|Et quorum tecta sunt peccata]], that is, hidden from the eyes of God, so that they are not seen, nor does he impute them, but turns away his face from them[[Ps 50:11||]], as if they had never been. Therefore it follows: [[4:8|Blessed is the man to whom the Lord hath not imputed sin|Beatus vir cui non imputavit nec imputat Dominus peccatum]], nor imputes it, but wholly pardons it, as he promised through Isaias: [[Is 44:22|I have blotted out thy iniquities as a cloud, and thy sins as a mist|Delebo ut nubem iniquitates tuas, et quasi caliginem peccata tua]] [Denis reads *Delebo*, "I will blot out"; the margin gives Is. xlv, 22].

paras.t: Applicans autem Apostolus scripturam hanc ad propositum suum, adjecit : Beatitudo ergo hæc, de qua loquitur David, in circumcisione tantum manet, id est, in solis Judæis locum habet, an etiam in præputio, id est gentilibus incircumcisis? Et hoc ideo quæro : Dicimus enim, quia reputata est Abrahæ fides ad justitiam, sicut nunc ex Genesi allegatum est. Quomodo ergo, id est in quo statu, reputata est Abrahæ fides ad justitiam? In circumcisione, hoc est pro statu et tempore circumcisionis suæ, an in præputio, id est tempore circumcisionem suam præcedente? Et respondet : Non in circumcisione, sed in præputio. Quod consequenter declarat. Et signum accepit circumcisionis, id est, ipsam circumcisionem accepit, Deo jubente, pro signo distinctivo inter ipsum et posteros suos fideles, ac inter infideles, et etiam pro signo fidei suæ, quam habuit ante circumcisionem. Circumcisio quippe fuit quædam protestatio fidei, definiturque sic : Circumcisio est signum distinguens Israel a gentibus. Patet ergo quod non frustra circumcisionem accepit, quamvis per eam justificatus non sit ex parte operis operati, sed operis operantis, videlicet fidei, devotionis ac obedientiæ, per quas abundantiorem justificationem adeptus est, quam ante habuerat. Unde Dominus loquebatur : Circumcidetis carnem præputii vestri, ut sit signum fœderis mei inter me et vos. Sic ergo accepit signum circumcisionis, quod est signaculum, id est indicium, justitiæ fidei, id est, quæ per fidem habetur, quæ est in præputio, id est in Abraham, vel ceteris gentilibus justis, sicut in Job, tempore præputii. Nam Abraham ante circumcisionem suam justus fuit, et credidit Deo, sicut jam dictum est. Ut sit pater spiritualis et imitatione condignus omnium credentium, non Judæorum dumtaxat, per præputium, id est in statu præputii : quia per fidem quam in præputio habuit, meruit spiritualem paternitatem omnium gentium. Vel, Omnium credentium per præputium, id est gentilium cum præputio ad fidem accedentium. Ut reputetur et illis, videlicet filiis Abrahæ, ad justitiam fidei, per quam ipsum Abraham assequuntur, sicut et ei reputata est. Et sit Abraham pater circumcisionis spiritualis (quæ in vitiorum eradicatione consistit), id est gentilium credentium : pater, inquam, præbendo exemplum, non conferendo justitiam, non his tantum, id est non solum ad profectum his, qui sunt ex circumcisione carnali, id est Judæis, sed et his qui sectantur vestigia fidei, id est universis fidelibus imitantibus fidem, quæ est in præputio patris nostri Abrahæ, id est, quæ erat in Abraham adhuc habente præputium; vel, Quæ est, id est, consideratur in eo nondum circumciso.
paras.en: Applying this scripture to his purpose, the Apostle added: [[4:9|This blessedness then|Beatitudo ergo hæc]], of which David speaks, [[4:9|doth it remain in the circumcision only|in circumcisione tantum manet]], that is, does it have place in the Jews alone, [[4:9|or in the uncircumcision also?|an etiam in præputio?]], that is, in the uncircumcised Gentiles? And I ask this for this reason: [[4:9|For we say that unto Abraham faith was reputed to justice|Dicimus enim, quia reputata est Abrahæ fides ad justitiam]], as has just been cited from Genesis[[4:3||]]. [[4:10|How then was it reputed?|Quomodo ergo reputata est?]], that is, in what state was faith reputed to Abraham unto justice? [[4:10|When he was in circumcision|In circumcisione]], that is, in the state and time of his circumcision, [[4:10|or in uncircumcision?|an in præputio?]], that is, in the time before his circumcision? And he answers: [[4:10|Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision|Non in circumcisione, sed in præputio]]. Which he then makes plain. [[4:11|And he received the sign of circumcision|Et signum accepit circumcisionis]], that is, he received circumcision itself at God's command, as a distinguishing sign between himself and his faithful posterity and the unbelievers, and also as a sign of his faith, which he had before circumcision. For circumcision was a kind of profession of faith, and is defined thus: circumcision is a sign distinguishing Israel from the Gentiles. It is plain, then, that he did not receive circumcision in vain, although he was not justified by it on the side of the work done, but of the worker's act, namely faith, devotion and obedience, through which he obtained a more abundant justification than he had had before. Hence the Lord said: [[Gen 17:11|And you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be for a sign of the covenant between me and you|Circumcidetis carnem præputii vestri, ut sit signum fœderis mei inter me et vos]]. So then he received the sign of circumcision, which is [[4:11|a seal of the justice of the faith|signaculum justitiæ fidei]], that is, a token of the justice which is had through faith, [[4:11|which he had, being uncircumcised|quæ est in præputio]], that is, in Abraham, or in the other just Gentiles, as in Job, in the time of uncircumcision. For Abraham was just before his circumcision, and believed God, as has just been said[[4:3||]]. [[4:11|that he might be the father|Ut sit pater]], spiritual and worthy of imitation, [[4:11|of all them that believe|omnium credentium]], not of the Jews only, [[4:11|being uncircumcised|per præputium]], that is, in the state of uncircumcision: because by the faith he had in uncircumcision he merited the spiritual fatherhood of all nations. Or, *of all them that believe being uncircumcised*, that is, of the Gentiles coming to the faith with uncircumcision. [[4:11|that unto them also it may be reputed to justice|ut reputetur et illis ad justitiam]], namely to the children of Abraham, the justice of faith, through which they follow Abraham himself, as it was reputed to him. [[4:12|And he might be the father of circumcision|Et sit Abraham pater circumcisionis]], the spiritual circumcision (which consists in rooting out vices), that is, of the believing Gentiles: a father, I say, by giving an example, not by conferring justice, [[4:12|not to them only|non his tantum]], that is, not only for the profit of those [[4:12|that are of the circumcision|qui sunt ex circumcisione]] in the flesh, that is, the Jews, [[4:12|but to them also that follow the steps of the faith|sed et his qui sectantur vestigia fidei]], that is, all the faithful who imitate the faith [[4:12|that is in the uncircumcision of our father Abraham|quæ est in præputio patris nostri Abrahæ]], that is, which was in Abraham while he still had his foreskin; or, *which is*, that is, is considered in him while not yet circumcised.

paras.t: Insuper manifestat Apostolus, quod Abraham pater sit spiritualis circumcisionis cunctis fidelibus per hoc quod consecutus est promissionem hereditatis, non ex operibus, sed merito fidei, quæ ad omnes electos communiter pertinet. Non enim per legem facta est promissio Abrahæ aut semini ejus, hoc est de multiplicatione seminis sui; vel, Semini ejus, id est Christo de semine Abrahæ nato, secundum naturam assumptam ; ut heres esset mundi, id est, ut ipse Abraham per semen suum, vel in semine suo, hoc est per Christum, possideret omnes terminos terræ, omnesque populos sæculi. Dictum enim est Abrahæ : In semine tuo benedicentur omnes tribus terræ; et iterum, Dilataberis ad orientem et occidentem, etc. Quum enim facta est Abrahæ ista promissio, nondum erat lex data, quam constat per Moysen datam. Hæc vero promissio maxime adimpleta est in Christo filio Abrahæ, qui de se ipso testatur: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo in terra. Ad quem Pater in Psalmo: Postula, inquit, a me, et dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam, et possessionem tuam terminos terræ. Sed per justitiam fidei, id est procedente ex fide, quæ erat in Abraham. Pro hac namque justitia et merito ejus, facta est Abrahæ præindulta promissio, sicut in Genesi legitur.
paras.en: Moreover the Apostle shows that Abraham is father of the spiritual circumcision to all the faithful, by this, that he obtained the promise of the inheritance, not by works, but by the merit of faith, which belongs to all the elect in common. [[4:13|For not through the law was the promise to Abraham or to his seed|Non enim per legem facta est promissio Abrahæ aut semini ejus]], that is, concerning the multiplying of his seed; or, *to his seed*, that is, to Christ born of the seed of Abraham according to the nature he assumed; [[4:13|that he should be heir of the world|ut heres esset mundi]], that is, that Abraham himself, through his seed, or in his seed, that is, through Christ, should possess all the ends of the earth and all the peoples of the world. For it was said to Abraham: [[Gen 22:18|in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|In semine tuo benedicentur omnes tribus terræ]]; and again, [[Gen 28:14|thou shalt spread abroad to the west, and to the east|Dilataberis ad orientem et occidentem]], etc. For when this promise was made to Abraham, the law had not yet been given, which it is certain was given through Moses[[John 1:17||]]. And this promise was fulfilled above all in Christ the son of Abraham, who testifies of himself: [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo in terra]]. To whom the Father says in the Psalm: [[Ps 2:8|Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance, and the utmost parts of the earth for thy possession|Postula, inquit, a me, et dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam, et possessionem tuam terminos terræ]]. [[4:13|but through the justice of faith|Sed per justitiam fidei]], that is, proceeding from the faith that was in Abraham. For because of this justice and its merit the promise spoken of was granted to Abraham, as we read in Genesis[[Gen 22:18||]].

paras.t: Si enim qui ex lege hi tantum heredes sunt, id est, si soli Judæi legem scriptam habentes, hereditatem seu gratiam benedictionis Abrahæ repromissam accipiunt; exinanita, hoc est frustrata est fides Abrahæ Deo credentis, qui prædixit: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes familiæ terræ; abolita, id est evacuata atque ablata, est promissio Dei Abrahæ facta de hereditatione mundi, et benedictione omnium gentium sæculi. Præterea, promissionem præfatam non esse ex lege, sed fide, ostendit Apostolus ex legis imperfectione. Lex enim iram operatur, id est, pœnæ obnoxium facit, quia legis transgressorem. Nam temporales pœnas determinat, et prævaricatorem legis magis damnabilem reddit eo qui non legem quam sortitus est legem. Dat enim manifestiorem notitiam culpæ, quam ante, sicque transgressionem efficit gravior. Propter quod in Evangelio dicitur: Servus qui cognovit voluntatem domini sui, et non fecit, plagis vapulabit multis. Ubi enim non est lex, prævaricatio. Si acceperimus legem communiter pro quacumque lege, videlicet naturali, scripta, vel evangelica, certum est sine lege non esse prævaricationem, quum prævaricatio sit transgressio legis. Si autem sumpserimus legem hoc loco pro lege scripta, dicendum erit quod non est lex, non est prævaricatio ubi ad eo gravis: quoniam lex occasionaliter auget peccatum, provocat iram, nec habuit gratiam, sicut ex dictis clarius ceteris.
paras.en: [[4:14|For if they who are of the law be heirs|Si enim qui ex lege hi tantum heredes sunt]] only, that is, if the Jews alone, having the written law, receive the inheritance, or the grace of the blessing promised to Abraham, [[4:14|faith is made void|exinanita est fides]], that is, frustrated, the faith of Abraham believing God, who foretold, In thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed[[Gen 22:18||]]; [[4:14|the promise is made of no effect|abolita est promissio]], that is, emptied and taken away, God's promise made to Abraham about inheriting the world and the blessing of all the nations of the world. Moreover, the Apostle shows from the imperfection of the law that the promise spoken of is not from the law but from faith. [[4:15|For the law worketh wrath|Lex enim iram operatur]], that is, makes a man liable to punishment, as a transgressor of the law. For it lays down temporal punishments, and makes the transgressor of the law more damnable than one who has not received the law. For it gives a clearer knowledge of the fault than before, and so makes the transgression heavier. For which reason it is said in the Gospel: [[Luke 12:47|that servant, who knew the will of his lord and prepared not himself and did not according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes|Servus qui cognovit voluntatem domini sui, et non fecit, plagis vapulabit multis]]. [[4:15|For where there is no law, neither is there transgression|Ubi enim non est lex, prævaricatio]]. If we take law in common for any law whatever, namely natural, written or evangelical, it is certain that without law there is no transgression, since transgression is the breaking of a law. But if we take law here for the written law, we must say that where there is no law there is not so grave a transgression: since the law occasionally increases sin, provokes wrath, and did not have grace, as is clearer from what has been said.

paras.t: Ideo ex fide, id est merito fidei, ut secundum gratiam Dei […] per opera legis, heredes effecti sunt divinæ promissionis omnes qui Abrahæ fidem sectati sunt, ut secundum gratiam Dei, non secundum justitias legis, firma sit promissio facta Abrahæ et semini ejus: firma, inquam, exsistat atque salubriter exhibeatur omni semini, id est universis fidelibus: non ei qui ex lege est solum, id est non tantum Judæis, carnalibus Abrahæ filiis, sed et ei qui ex fide est Abrahæ, id est cunctis quoque gentilibus Abrahæ fidem sequentibus. Si enim ista promissio fundaretur in lege, quæ occasionaliter operatur et provocat iram, non haberet stabilitatem, quia lege transgressa retractaretur. Nunc vero quia fundatur in fide viri constantis, videlicet Abrahæ, magis tamen in gratia Dei, permanet firma omni semini Abrahæ. Qui pater est spiritualis, seu exemplaris institutor ad fidem, omnium nostrum, id est cunctorum credentium, sicut scriptum est in Genesi, quantum ad sensum: Quia patrem spiritualem (ut dictum est) multarum gentium posui, id est institui, te ante Deum, id est coram Deo, videlicet me ipso, cui credidisti loquenti tibi per angelum in persona Dei, qui vivificat mortuos corporaliter, animas corporibus reuniendo, et spiritualiter, gratiam peccatoribus conferendo. Unde scriptum est: Pater suscitat mortuos et vivificat. Et vocat a non esse ad esse, ea quæ non sunt, id est creanda, tanquam ea quæ sunt, id est, sicut existentia vocantur ad aliquid. Sic enim Deo imperante, dicente seu vocante producuntur multa ex nihilo, id est tam facile ac obedienter ac si ex præjacenti aliquo fierent, atque jam essent. Vel sic: Vocat ad fidem et gratiam, ea quæ non sunt, id est gentes, qui coram Deo quasi nihil fuerunt, quia spiritualiter mortui erant, quemadmodum in Isaia scribitur: Omnes gentes quasi non sunt, sic sunt coram eo, et quasi nihilum et inane reputatae sunt ei: […], id est, sicut vocavit Judæos, qui propter legem et gratiam Dei aliquid erant, spiritualiter coram Deo viventes.
paras.en: [[4:16|Therefore is it of faith|Ideo ex fide]], that is, by the merit of faith, that according to the grace of God [… a line is lost here in the transcription …] by the works of the law, all who have followed the faith of Abraham have been made heirs of the divine promise, [[4:16|that according to grace|ut secundum gratiam]] of God, not according to the justices of the law, [[4:16|the promise might be firm|firma sit promissio]] made to Abraham and his seed: firm, I say, may it stand and be shown forth for salvation [[4:16|to all the seed|omni semini]], that is, to all the faithful: [[4:16|not to that only which is of the law|non ei qui ex lege est solum]], that is, not only to the Jews, the carnal children of Abraham, [[4:16|but to that also which is of the faith of Abraham|sed et ei qui ex fide est Abrahæ]], that is, to all the Gentiles too who follow the faith of Abraham. For if this promise were founded on the law, which occasionally works and provokes wrath, it would have no stability, because when the law was transgressed it would be withdrawn. But now because it is founded on the faith of a steadfast man, namely Abraham, but more on the grace of God, it remains firm for all the seed of Abraham. [[4:16|who is the father of us all|qui pater est omnium nostrum]], the spiritual father, or the exemplary founder in faith, that is, of all believers, [[4:17|As it is written|sicut scriptum est]] in Genesis, as to the sense: [[4:17|I have made thee a father of many nations|Quia patrem … multarum gentium posui … te]][[Gen 17:5||]], a spiritual father (as has been said), *I have made*, that is, appointed, [[4:17|before God|ante Deum]], that is, in the sight of God, namely myself, [[4:17|whom he believed|cui credidisti]], *whom thou didst believe* when he spoke to thee through an angel in the person of God, [[4:17|who quickeneth the dead|qui vivificat mortuos]] bodily, by reuniting souls to bodies, and spiritually, by conferring grace on sinners. Hence it is written: [[John 5:21|the Father raiseth up the dead and giveth life|Pater suscitat mortuos et vivificat]]. [[4:17|and calleth|Et vocat]] from not being to being [[4:17|those things that are not|ea quæ non sunt]], that is, things to be created, [[4:17|as those that are|tanquam ea quæ sunt]], that is, as existing things are called to something. For so, at God's command, word or call, many things are brought forth from nothing, that is, as easily and obediently as if they were being made from something lying ready and already existed. Or thus: *he calleth* to faith and grace *those things that are not*, that is, the Gentiles, who were as nothing before God, because they were spiritually dead, as it is written in Isaias: [[Is 40:17|All nations are before him as if they had no being at all, and are counted to him as nothing, and vanity|Omnes gentes quasi non sunt, sic sunt coram eo, et quasi nihilum et inane reputatae sunt ei]]: […], that is, as he called the Jews, who because of the law and the grace of God were something, living spiritually before God.

paras.t: Qui Abraham contra spem naturæ in spem gratiæ credidit, credens posse impleri per gratiam, quod erat impossibile per naturam, ut scilicet ipse jam vetulus, de infecunda ac sterili conjuge sua filium procrearet, ut fieret pater multarum gentium eum per fidem sequentium, secundum quod dictum est ei a Deo per angelum : Sic erit semen tuum, sicut stellæ cœli in multitudine, et sicut arena quæ est in littore maris, id est, præ multitudine numerari non poterit. Quamvis hoc aliquo modo videatur impletum in carnali semine Abrahæ, quia et Moyses filiis Israel aiebat, Estis hodie sicut stellæ cœli plurimi ; verius tamen atque perfectius in spirituali semine ejus, id est in gentium conversione et fidelium multiplicatione, impletur, præsertim quum rursus Moyses dicat populo Judæorum : Te elegit Dominus, non quia cunctas gentes numero vincebatis, quum sitis omnibus populis pauciores. Vel hoc quod dicitur, Sicut stellæ cœli, refertur ad bonos : qui stellis comparantur propter lumen gratiæ, decorem virtutum, et quoniam alios verbo et operatione illustrant, ipsamque Ecclesiam ornant quemadmodum stellæ cœlum. Propter quod in alia epistola ait Apostolus : Inter quos lucetis sicut luminaria mundi. Quod vero adjungitur, Et sicut arena maris, referri potest ad malos, terrenis rebus intentos.
paras.en: [[4:18|Who against hope believed in hope|Qui … contra spem … in spem … credidit]], Abraham, against the hope of nature, in the hope of grace, believing that what was impossible by nature could be fulfilled by grace, namely that he, already old, should beget a son of his barren and sterile wife, [[4:18|that he might be made the father of many nations|ut fieret pater multarum gentium]] who follow him through faith, [[4:18|according to that which was said to him|secundum quod dictum est ei]] by God through an angel: [[Gen 15:5|So shall thy seed be|Sic erit semen tuum]], as the stars of heaven in multitude, and as the sand that is on the seashore[[Gen 22:17||]], that is, for multitude it could not be numbered. Although this seems in some way fulfilled in the carnal seed of Abraham, since Moses too said to the children of Israel, [[Deut 1:10|you are this day as the stars of heaven, for multitude|Estis hodie sicut stellæ cœli plurimi]]; yet it is fulfilled more truly and perfectly in his spiritual seed, that is, in the conversion of the Gentiles and the multiplying of the faithful, especially since Moses again says to the people of the Jews: [[Deut 7:7|Not because you surpass all nations in number|non quia cunctas gentes numero vincebatis]] hath the Lord chosen you, [[Deut 7:7|for you are the fewest of any people|quum sitis omnibus populis pauciores]]. Or what is said, *as the stars of heaven*, refers to the good, who are compared to the stars[[Dan 12:3||]] for the light of grace, the beauty of the virtues, and because they enlighten others by word and work, and adorn the Church as the stars the sky. For which reason the Apostle says in another epistle: [[Phil 2:15|among whom you shine as lights in the world|Inter quos lucetis sicut luminaria mundi]]. And what is added, *and as the sand of the sea*, may be referred to the wicked, intent on earthly things.

paras.t: Et non est Abraham infirmatus in fide, ex consideratione naturalis impossibilitatis, nec consideravit cum superflua immoratione seu finali sistentia, corpus suum jam emortuum a virtute generativa, quum jam fere centum esset annorum, et emortuam vulvam Saræ, id est ad actum generationis ineptam : desierant enim ei muliebria fieri, sine quibus naturaliter non fit conceptio. — Videtur his obviare, quod in Genesi legitur Abraham post mortem Saræ Ceturam duxisse. atque multos de ea filios genuisse, elapsis plus quam triginta septem annis a tempore generationis seu promissionis Isaac. Sara quippe decem annis junior fuerat eo. Quum ergo ipsa defuncta sit centum viginti septem annis expletis, certum est Abraham plus quam centum triginta septem annorum fuisse, quando Ceturam sumpsit uxorem. Quomodo ergo emortuum erat corpus ejus quum centenarius circiter fuit? Communiter respondetur, quod emortuum erat quantum ad vetulam, non quantum ad juniorem, quæ facilius concipit anu, propter dispositionem virtutis passivæ.
paras.en: [[4:19|And he was not weak in faith|Et non est Abraham infirmatus in fide]] from considering the natural impossibility, [[4:19|Neither did he consider|nec consideravit]] with needless dwelling on it, or with a final halting there, [[4:19|his own body, now dead|corpus suum jam emortuum]] as to the power of begetting, [[4:19|(whereas he was almost an hundred years old), nor the dead womb of Sara|quum jam fere centum esset annorum, et emortuam vulvam Saræ]], that is, unfit for the act of generation: for it had ceased to be with her after the manner of women[[Gen 18:11||]], without which conception does not naturally take place. Against this seems to be what we read in Genesis, that Abraham after Sara's death took Cetura and begot many sons of her[[Gen 25:1||]][[Gen 25:2||]], more than thirty-seven years after the time of the begetting, or the promise, of Isaac. For Sara was ten years younger than he[[Gen 17:17||]]. Since then she died having completed a hundred and twenty-seven years[[Gen 23:1||]], it is certain that Abraham was more than a hundred and thirty-seven years old when he took Cetura to wife. How then was his body dead when he was about a hundred? The common answer is that it was dead as regards an old woman, not as regards a younger one, who conceives more easily than an old woman because of the disposition of the passive power.

paras.t: In repromissione etiam Dei sibi facta de generatione Isaac, et innumerabili multitudine seminis sui, non hæsitavit diffidentia propter rei novitatem ; sed confortatus est fide, dans gloriam Deo, id est, Deum glorificans atque collaudans, tanquam omnipotentem ac verum, et ista implere valentem, et plenissime sciens, etiam per naturalem rationem, quia quæcumque promisit Deus, potens est et facere. Alias esset in promittendo improvidus, et in exsequendo infirmus. Ideo et reputatum est illi ad justitiam, quod sic confortatus est in fide, nec hæsitavit diffidentia. — Quod autem Abraham aliquo modo consideravit corpus suum et Saræ esse emortuum, patet ex eo quod dicebat : Putasne centenario nascetur filius, et Sara nonagenaria pariet? Verum, ut dixi, non sistebat finaliter in consideratione hujusmodi, sed in consideratione virtutis divinæ. Ex prædictis autem verbis dubitasse videtur. Respondetur communiter, quod non dubitando, sed admirando hæc dixit. Verumtamen videtur adhuc contrariari, quod per Isaiam Dominus loquitur Israeli : Pater tuus primus peccavit. Quod non solum quidam præcipui Judæorum magistri, sed sanctus quoque Hieronymus exponit de Abraham, quod peccavit ex incredulitate ridendo atque dicendo verba inducta. Sed sicut in expositione Isaiæ audens non eram, quantum ad hoc, sequi Hieronymum, ita nec modo: nec etiam nego. Apostolus enim apertissime contestatur, quod non hæsitavit diffidentia, et ideo reputatum sit ei ad justitiam. Unde verbum Isaiæ exponi potest de primo parente, videlicet Adam, quem constat in paradiso peccasse.
paras.en: [[4:20|In the promise also of God|In repromissione etiam Dei]] made to him about the begetting of Isaac and the innumerable multitude of his seed [[4:20|he staggered not by distrust|non hæsitavit diffidentia]] because of the newness of the thing; [[4:20|but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God|sed confortatus est fide, dans gloriam Deo]], that is, glorifying and praising God as almighty and true, and able to fulfil these things, [[4:21|Most fully knowing|et plenissime sciens]], even by natural reason, [[4:21|that whatsoever he has promised, he is able also to perform|quia quæcumque promisit Deus, potens est et facere]]. Otherwise he would be improvident in promising and weak in carrying out. [[4:22|And therefore it was reputed to him unto justice|Ideo et reputatum est illi ad justitiam]], that he was so strengthened in faith and did not stagger by distrust. That Abraham in some way considered his own body and Sara's to be dead is plain from his saying: [[Gen 17:17|Shall a son, thinkest thou, be born to him that is a hundred years old? and shall Sara that is ninety years old bring forth?|Putasne centenario nascetur filius, et Sara nonagenaria pariet?]] But, as I said, he did not halt finally in such a consideration, but in the consideration of the divine power. From the words spoken he seems to have doubted. The common answer is that he said these things not doubting but wondering. Yet there still seems to be a contradiction in what the Lord says to Israel through Isaias: [[Is 43:27|Thy first father sinned|Pater tuus primus peccavit]]. Which not only certain leading masters of the Jews, but holy Jerome too, expound of Abraham, that he sinned from unbelief in laughing and saying the words quoted[[Gen 17:17||]]. But as in the exposition of Isaias I did not dare follow Jerome in this, so neither now: nor do I deny it. For the Apostle most openly testifies that he did not stagger by distrust, and that therefore it was reputed to him unto justice. Hence the word of Isaias may be expounded of the first parent, namely Adam, who it is certain sinned in paradise[[Gen 3:6||]].

paras.t: Non est autem scriptum tantum propter ipsum Abraham istud, scilicet quia reputatum est illi ad justitiam, quod tam firmiter credidit; sed et propter nos, id est ad nostram consolationem ac instructionem, ut imitemur fidem ipsius, quibus reputabitur ad justitiam imitatio fidei Abrahæ, credentibus in eum qui suscitavit a mortuis Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum, id est in Deum Patrem seu sanctam Trinitatem, vel quamcumque divinam Personam. Cuilibet namque divinæ Personæ attribui potest suscitatio activa Christi: imo ipse ut Deus, suscіtavit se ipsum ut homo est. Et qui credit in unam divinam Personam, credit in tres.
paras.en: [[4:23|Now it is not written only for him. that it was reputed to him unto justice|Non est autem scriptum tantum propter ipsum Abraham istud, scilicet quia reputatum est illi ad justitiam]], Abraham, namely this, that he believed so firmly; [[4:24|But also for us|sed et propter nos]], that is, for our consolation and instruction, that we may imitate his faith, [[4:24|to whom it shall be reputed|quibus reputabitur]] unto justice, the imitation of Abraham's faith, [[4:24|if we believe in him that raised up Jesus Christ, our Lord, from the dead|credentibus in eum qui suscitavit a mortuis Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum]], that is, in God the Father, or the holy Trinity, or any divine Person. For the active raising of Christ can be attributed to any divine Person: indeed he himself as God raised himself as he is man. And he who believes in one divine Person believes in three.

paras.t: Qui Christus traditus est propter delicta nostra, id est morti expositus, ut mundi peccata auferret. Traditus est autem a Patre, juxta illud : Proprio filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum. Saltem permissive tradidit quoque se ipsum, secundum quod per Prophetam dicitur : Tradidit in mortem animam suam. Sed et Judas tradidit eum. Et resurrexit propter justificationem nostram, hoc est, ut virtute suæ resurrectionis gratiam justificantem nobis conferret, et suæ corporalis resurrectionis exemplo nos ad spiritualem resurrectionem induceret, quatenus tandem etiam corporaliter feliciterque resuscitemur ab ipso, quando reformabit corpus humilitatis nostræ, configuratum corpori claritatis suæ. Resurrexit ergo propter justificationem nostram, id est, ut justificemur gratiam recipiendo, et juste vivendo. Non tamen justificatio nostra est tota ratio finisque totalis resurrectionis Christi. Resurrexit namque propter proprii corporis glorificationem, et suæ humanitatis reassociationem, quantum ad partium ejus redintegrationem. Denique resurrexit propter justificationem nostram, quia ad hoc resurrexit, ut corpore resumpto, appareat nunc vultui Dei pro nobis, ostendens Patri latus et vulnera, quatenus merito ejus, gratia impleamur divina. Quamvis autem sit traditus Christus, non solum propter delicta nostra, sed etiam propter justificationem nostram (nam et propter utrumque surrexit), traditio tamen seu passio attribuitur delicto, ut mors naturæ correspondeat morti culpæ, et resurrectio justificationi, ut corporis glorificatio correspondeat novæ atque cœlesti conversationi.
paras.en: [[4:25|Who was delivered up for our sins|Qui Christus traditus est propter delicta nostra]], Christ, that is, exposed to death, to take away the sins of the world. And he was delivered up by the Father, according to that: [[Rom 8:32|He that spared not even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all|Proprio filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum]]. At least permissively; he also delivered up himself, according as it is said through the Prophet: [[Is 53:12|he hath delivered his soul unto death|Tradidit in mortem animam suam]]. And Judas too delivered him up[[Matt 26:47||]]. [[4:25|and rose again for our justification|Et resurrexit propter justificationem nostram]], that is, so that by the power of his resurrection he might confer justifying grace on us, and by the example of his bodily resurrection lead us to spiritual resurrection, so that at last we may also be raised bodily and happily by him, when he will reform [[Phil 3:21|the body of our lowness, made like to the body of his glory|corpus humilitatis nostræ, configuratum corpori claritatis suæ]]. He rose again, then, for our justification, that is, that we may be justified by receiving grace and living justly. Yet our justification is not the whole reason and entire end of Christ's resurrection. For he rose again for the glorifying of his own body, and the re-uniting of his manhood, as to the restoring of its parts. Lastly, he rose again for our justification because he rose to this end, that, having taken up his body again, he may [[Heb 9:24|appear now in the presence of God for us|appareat nunc vultui Dei pro nobis]], showing the Father his side and wounds, so that by his merit we may be filled with divine grace. And although Christ was delivered up not only for our sins but also for our justification (for he rose again for both), yet the delivering, or passion, is attributed to sin, so that the death of nature may answer to the death of fault, and the resurrection to justification, so that the glorifying of the body may answer to the new and heavenly way of life.

5.title: Declaratio capituli quinti: Justificati ergo ex fide.
5.title_en: Declaration of the fifth chapter: Being justified therefore by faith.
5.note: A few lines are missing from the transcription (in verses 1, 8–9, 13, 17 and 19); they await a scan of the page.

paras.t: Postquam Apostolus abstulit causam atque materiam discordiæ Romanorum, jam eos invitat ad veram pacem, et ait: Justificati ergo, id est justi a Deo effecti, ex fide, id est per fidei formatæ infusionem; vel, Justificati, id est veram justitiam operati, ex fide, id est per habitum fidei; vel, intus in anima justificati sine opere exteriori, ex fide, id est, interiori fidei actu credendo, videlicet ex caritate, et non per opera legis, neque per opera præcedentia fidem, […] beamus ad Deum, id est, Deo humiliter subditi simus, et nostram voluntatem divinæ ordinationi in omnibus subjiciamus, quieti atque tranquilli exsistentes in Deo. Beati enim pacifici, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur. Hinc enim loquitur Scriptura: Acquiesce Deo, et habeto pacem, et per hoc habebis fructus optimos. Hæc est spiritualis divinaque pax de qua dixerunt angeli: Pax hominibus bonæ voluntatis; et David, Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam. Quæ non competit impiis, juxta illud Isaiæ: Non est pax impiis, dicit Dominus. Per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, quia per eum seu merito ejus pacem istam consequimur. Omnia namque divinarum gratiarum charismata per Christum, secundum quod mediator est Dei et hominum, præstantur hominibus. Ideo subditur:
paras.en: After the Apostle has taken away the cause and matter of the Romans' discord, he now invites them to true peace, and says: [[5:1|Being justified therefore|Justificati ergo]], that is, made just by God, [[5:1|by faith|ex fide]], that is, by the infusion of formed faith; or, *being justified*, that is, having worked true justice, *by faith*, that is, through the habit of faith; or, justified inwardly in the soul without outward work, *by faith*, that is, by the inward act of faith in believing, namely from charity, and not through the works of the law, nor through works that go before faith, […] [a line or two is missing from the transcription here] [[5:1|let us have peace with God|pacem habeamus ad Deum]], that is, let us be humbly subject to God and submit our will to the divine ordering in all things, being quiet and at rest in God. For [[Matt 5:9|Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God|Beati enim pacifici, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur]]. Hence the Scripture says: [[Job 22:21|Submit thyself then to him, and be at peace: and thereby thou shalt have the best fruits|Acquiesce Deo, et habeto pacem, et per hoc habebis fructus optimos]]. This is the spiritual and divine peace of which the angels said: [[Luke 2:14|peace to men of good will|Pax hominibus bonæ voluntatis]]; and David: [[Ps 118:165|Much peace have they that love thy law|Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam]]. Which does not belong to the wicked, according to that word of Isaias: [[Is 48:22|There is no peace to the wicked, saith the Lord|Non est pax impiis, dicit Dominus]]. [[5:1|Through our Lord Jesus Christ|Per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum]], since through him, or by his merit, we obtain this peace. For all the gifts of the divine graces are bestowed on men through Christ, inasmuch as he is [[1 Tim 2:5|mediator of God and men|mediator est Dei et hominum]]. Therefore there follows:

paras.t: Per quem, tanquam per mediatorem et causam meritoriam, accessum, hoc est ingressum, habemus per fidem, tanquam per fundamentum totius spiritualis ædificii (accedentem nempe ad Deum oportet credere), in gratiam istam, id est ad dona et munera Spiritus Sancti, videlicet ad alias perfectiones seu beneficia Dei; in qua gratia stamus, mente ad divina erecta atque cœlestia diligente, non in terrenis jacente vilibusque immersa. Primo enim Deus quum fidem infundit, donat simul tempore alias virtutes ac dona Spiritus Sancti. Fides tamen præcedit secundum viam generationis, et ordine naturæ, quum sit fundamentum virtutum: et ita per fidem, accessum habemus ad alia bona. Fide autem infusa, per eamdem fidem accedimus ad Deum, ut gratiam ampliorem mereamur, quatenus proficiscamur de virtute in virtutem, id est, de bono in melius proficiendo quotidie. Et gloriamur spirituali lætitia in spe gloriæ, id est in certa exspectatione felicitatis æternæ, quæ est gloria filiorum Dei, id est omnium Beatorum Deo fruentium, qui Deo perfectissime similantur. De quibus scriptum est in Job: Ubi eras quum me laudarent astra matutina, et jubilarent omnes filii Dei? Et in Psalmo: Quoniam quis in nubibus æquabitur Domino, similis erit Domino in filiis Dei? Possunt tamen per filios Dei intelligi omnes electi, ad vitam æternam præordinati. Et certe, hoc merito esse debet nobis indeficiens ratio gloriandi, quod spem habemus acquirendi beatitudinem sempiternam. Unde nihil Christiano felicius, cui promittuntur regna cœlorum.
paras.en: [[5:2|By whom|Per quem]], as by the mediator and meritorious cause, [[5:2|we have access|accessum habemus]], that is, entrance, [[5:2|through faith|per fidem]], as through the foundation of the whole spiritual building (for [[Heb 11:6|he that cometh to God must believe|accedentem nempe ad Deum oportet credere]]), [[5:2|into this grace|in gratiam istam]], that is, to the gifts and bounties of the Holy Ghost, namely to the other perfections or benefits of God; [[5:2|wherein we stand|in qua gratia stamus]], in which grace we stand, with the mind raised up to divine things and loving the heavenly, not lying among earthly things and sunk in what is base. For first, when God infuses faith, he gives at the same time the other virtues and the gifts of the Holy Ghost. Yet faith goes before in the way of generation and in the order of nature, since it is the foundation of the virtues: and so through faith we have access to the other goods. And once faith has been infused, through the same faith we draw near to God, that we may merit fuller grace, so that we may go from virtue to virtue, that is, advancing daily from good to better. [[5:2|And glory|Et gloriamur]], with spiritual joy, [[5:2|in the hope of the glory|in spe gloriæ]], that is, in the sure expectation of eternal happiness, which is the glory [[5:2|of the sons of God|filiorum Dei]], that is, of all the Blessed who enjoy God, who are made most perfectly like God. Of whom it is written in Job: [[Job 38:7|When the morning stars praised me together, and all the sons of God made a joyful melody?|Ubi eras quum me laudarent astra matutina, et jubilarent omnes filii Dei?]] [Denis begins "Where wast thou when...", from the verse before]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 88:7|For who in the clouds can be compared to the Lord: or who among the sons of God shall be like to God?|Quoniam quis in nubibus æquabitur Domino, similis erit Domino in filiis Dei?]] But by the sons of God can also be understood all the elect, foreordained to eternal life. And surely this must rightly be for us an unfailing reason for glorying, that we have the hope of gaining everlasting beatitude. Hence nothing is happier than a Christian, to whom the kingdom of heaven is promised.

paras.t: Non solum autem gloriamur in spe gloriæ, credentes videre bona Domini in terra viventium, sed et gloriamur in tribulationibus, id est in adversis, in persecutionibus, tentationibus, ac ægrotationibus, quemadmodum per Jacobum inducitur: Omne gaudium existimate, fratres, quum in diversas tentationes incideritis. Et Salvator: Gaudete, inquit, et exsultate in illa hora, quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in cœlo. Debemus enim gaudere de hoc, quod sumus in via perveniendi ad Deum. Sed hæc est via salutis, multipliciter tribulari. Per multas quippe tribulationes oportet nos intrare in regnum cœlorum. Et merito in tribulationibus gloriamur, scientes quod tribulatio patientiam operatur, hoc est, actum patientiæ efficit in anima, scilicet sufferentiam, tanquam objectum mediatum virtutis quæ patientia nominatur. Si enim non esset tribulatio, nec patientia. Habitum quoque patientiæ firmat in anima. Patientia quippe quum sit virtus moralis, immediate versatur circa passionem animæ, puta tristitiam, quam ordinat. Deinde respicit actum, videlicet ipsam adversitatis tolerantiam, quam accidenter et occasionaliter inducit seu efficit tribulatio. Frequens namque tribulatio confert animæ consuetudinem patientiam exercendi: et ita fit anima in virtute patientiæ inconcussa atque immobilis, ita ut dulce sit ei, tribulationem pro Dei amore, et propriorum peccatorum purgatione sufferre.
paras.en: [[5:3|And not only so|Non solum autem]] do we glory in the hope of glory, believing [[Ps 26:13|to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living|videre bona Domini in terra viventium]], [[5:3|but we glory also in tribulation|sed et gloriamur in tribulationibus]], that is, in adversities, persecutions, temptations and sicknesses, as is set down by James: [[Jas 1:2|count it all joy, when you shall fall into divers temptations|Omne gaudium existimate, fratres, quum in diversas tentationes incideritis]]. And the Saviour says: [[Luke 6:23|Be glad in that day and rejoice: for behold, your reward is great in heaven|Gaudete, inquit, et exsultate in illa hora, quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in cœlo]][[Matt 5:12||]] [Denis's wording mixes Luke 6:23 and Matt 5:12]. For we ought to rejoice in this, that we are on the way of coming to God. But this is the way of salvation: to be troubled in many ways. For [[Acts 14:21|through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God|Per multas quippe tribulationes oportet nos intrare in regnum cœlorum]] [Denis: "of heaven"]. And rightly do we glory in tribulations, [[5:3|knowing that tribulation worketh patience|scientes quod tribulatio patientiam operatur]][[Jas 1:3||]], that is, produces the act of patience in the soul, namely endurance, as the mediate object of the virtue called patience. For if there were no tribulation, there would be no patience. It also makes firm the habit of patience in the soul. For patience, being a moral virtue, is concerned immediately with a passion of the soul, namely sadness, which it orders. Then it looks to the act, namely the very bearing of adversity, which tribulation brings about or produces accidentally and as an occasion. For frequent tribulation gives the soul the custom of exercising patience: and so the soul becomes unshaken and immovable in the virtue of patience, so that it is sweet to it to bear tribulation for the love of God and the cleansing of its own sins.

paras.t: Patientia autem, id est adversitatum æquanimis tolerantia, operatur probationem, id est boni assuefactionem seu probam exercitationem, vel vitiorum expurgationem, etiam quoad pœnæ ablationem. Sicut enim interior dolor sive contritio aufert culpam, sic adversitatis perpessio pœnam. Probatio vero operatur vel efficit spem, id est actum spei, videlicet certam et actualem exspectationem felicitatis futuræ. Qui enim ita probatus est, fiducialiter præstolatur vitam æternam, juxta illud Salvatoris: Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum: et illud Sapientis, Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit electos Dominus, et in tempore erit respectus eorum. Porro habitus spei quum est virtus theologica, a solo Deo per creationem infunditur, sed actus ejus procedit partim ex meritis.
paras.en: [[5:4|And patience|Patientia autem]], that is, the even-minded bearing of adversities, works [[5:4|trial|probationem]], that is, the habit of good or a sound exercise, or the cleansing away of vices, even as to the removal of punishment. For as inward sorrow or contrition takes away guilt, so the suffering of adversity takes away punishment. [[5:4|And trial|Probatio vero]] works or produces [[5:4|hope|spem]], that is, the act of hope, namely the sure and actual expectation of future happiness. For he who has been so tried waits confidently for eternal life, according to the word of the Saviour: [[Matt 5:10|Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven|Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum]]; and that of the Wise man: [[Wis 3:6|As gold in the furnace, he hath proved them|Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit electos Dominus]] [Denis: "the Lord hath proved the elect"] … [[Wis 3:6|and in time there shall be respect had to them|et in tempore erit respectus eorum]]. Further, the habit of hope, being a theological virtue, is infused by God alone, by creation; but its act proceeds partly from merits. [in this part of the page the transcription has lost the last letters of each line of the left column; they have been restored where the sense is certain]

paras.t: Spes autem non confundit, id est sperantem non fallit, nec bono sperato defraudat, sicque erubescentiam tollit. Unde ait Scriptura: Nullus speravit in Domino, et confusus est; et Psalmista, Etenim universi qui sustinent te, non confundentur. Per Isaiam quoque Dominus loquitur: Ego Dominus, super quo non confundentur omnes qui exspectant eum. Oportet autem firmiter inviolabiliter sperare, ut dicamus cum sancto Job: Etiam si occiderit me, in ipso sperabo. Quod autem spes non confundat, sed impleatur, patet per hoc, quia caritas Dei, quæ est virtus theologica supernaturalis, summa ac divinissima, qua Deum proximumque diligimus, mandata implemus, unum cum Deo efficimur, et quidquid petierimus, obtinemus, diffusa, id est late ac liberaliter fusa, est in cordibus nostris, præsertim in voluntate, quæ est caritatis subjectum, per Spiritum Sanctum, id est a Spiritu Sancto, cui appropriatur bonitas, liberalitas, clementia, communicatio, et per consequens caritatis infusio, qui datus est nobis a Patre et Filio, imo et a se ipso, tanquam pignus et arrha felicitatis æternæ. Ipse enim Spiritus Sanctus est dator ac donum, procedítque a Patre ac Filio per modum donabilis, quoniam ipse est caritas seu amor Patris et Filii. Amor autem est primum donum gratuitum, in quo omnia dona donantur. Itaque Spiritus Sanctus datur electis, non solum in suo dono, sed etiam in se ipso, quia per caritatem habetur, et est in nobis novo specialique modo. Propter quod ait Salvator: Ego rogabo Patrem, et alium Paracletum dabit vobis, ut maneat vobiscum in æternum, Spiritum veritatis. Et in Actibus Apostolorum legitur, quod per impositionem manuum Apostolorum dabatur Spiritus Sanctus. Unde secundum B. Thomam in prima parte, et super primum Sententiarum, Persona divina dicitur esse alicujus dupliciter: Primo, ratione originis: et ita est ejus a quo procedit. Sicque Filius et Spiritus Sanctus sunt Patris, et Spiritus Sanctus est Filii. Secundo, ratione fruitionis seu communionis: et sic est ejus a quo habetur, id est intellectualis creaturæ, quæ libere frui potest Persona divina. Sic ergo Spiritus Sanctus datus est nobis, et est noster.
paras.en: [[5:5|And hope confoundeth not|Spes autem non confundit]], that is, does not deceive him who hopes, nor cheat him of the good hoped for, and so takes away shame. Hence the Scripture says: [[Ecclus 2:11|no one hath hoped in the Lord, and hath been confounded|Nullus speravit in Domino, et confusus est]] [the margin gives Ps 21:6; the words are those of Ecclus 2:11]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 24:3|none of them that wait on thee shall be confounded|Etenim universi qui sustinent te, non confundentur]] [the margin reads Ps. xxxiv, 3; the words are those of Ps 24:3]. Through Isaias too the Lord says: [[Is 49:23|I am the Lord, for they shall not be confounded that wait for him|Ego Dominus, super quo non confundentur omnes qui exspectant eum]]. We must hope firmly and inviolably, so as to say with holy Job: [[Job 13:15|Although he should kill me, I will trust in him|Etiam si occiderit me, in ipso sperabo]]. That hope does not confound, but is fulfilled, is plain from this, [[5:5|because the charity of God|quia caritas Dei]], which is the supernatural theological virtue, highest and most divine, by which we love God and our neighbour, fulfil the commandments, are made one with God and obtain whatever we ask[[John 15:7||]], [[5:5|is poured forth|diffusa, id est]], that is, poured out widely and generously, [[5:5|in our hearts|in cordibus nostris]], especially in the will, which is the subject of charity, [[5:5|by the Holy Ghost|per Spiritum Sanctum]], that is, from the Holy Ghost, to whom are appropriated goodness, generosity, clemency, communication, and consequently the infusion of charity, [[5:5|who is given to us|qui datus est nobis]] by the Father and the Son, nay, by himself too, as the pledge and earnest of eternal happiness. For the Holy Ghost himself is the giver and the gift, and proceeds from the Father and the Son in the manner of what can be given, since he is the charity or love of the Father and the Son. And love is the first free gift, in which all gifts are given. So the Holy Ghost is given to the elect not only in his gift but also in himself, since he is possessed through charity and is in us in a new and special way. For which reason the Saviour says: [[John 14:16|I will ask the Father: and he shall give you another Paraclete, that he may abide with you for ever|Ego rogabo Patrem, et alium Paracletum dabit vobis, ut maneat vobiscum in æternum]], [[John 14:17|The spirit of truth|Spiritum veritatis]]. And in the Acts of the Apostles we read that by the laying on of the Apostles' hands the Holy Ghost was given[[Acts 8:17||]]. Hence, according to Blessed Thomas in the First Part and on the First Book of the Sentences, a divine Person is said to be someone's in two ways. First, by reason of origin: and so he is his from whom he proceeds. Thus the Son and the Holy Ghost are the Father's, and the Holy Ghost is the Son's. Secondly, by reason of enjoyment or communion: and so he is his by whom he is possessed, that is, of the intellectual creature, which can freely enjoy a divine Person. In this way, then, the Holy Ghost has been given to us and is ours.

paras.t: Consequenter Apostolus tangit nostræ justificationis motivum: prosequitur quoque nostræ reconciliationis modum, et ait: Ut quid enim, id est, propter quid aliud, nisi ut Spiritus Sanctus nobis donetur, caritas Dei in cordibus nostris diffundatur, et spes impleatur, Christus, quum adhuc infirmi, id est vulneribus animæ sauciati, pœnis ac culpis adstricti, essemus secundum tempus, id est, antequam ab eo liberaremur ac purgaremur, pro impiis, id est pro nobis injustis et miseris, mortuus est? Vel illud, Secundum tempus, refertur ad id quod sequitur, Mortuus est: ut sit sensus, Mortuus est secundum tempus, id est per triduum sepulturæ. Tanquam dicat: Hoc magnum est valde atque mirabile, quod Christus pro nobis infirmis ac impiis mori dignatus est, quum ipse sit virtus Dei et Sanctus Sanctorum.
paras.en: Next the Apostle touches on the motive of our justification, and goes on to the manner of our reconciliation, saying: [[5:6|For why|Ut quid enim]], that is, for what else than that the Holy Ghost might be given to us, the charity of God poured forth in our hearts, and hope fulfilled, [[5:6|did Christ, when as yet we were weak|Christus, cum adhuc infirmi essemus]], that is, wounded with the wounds of the soul, bound by punishments and guilt, [[5:6|according to the time|secundum tempus]], that is, before we were freed and cleansed by him, [[5:6|die for the ungodly?|pro impiis mortuus est?]] that is, for us, unjust and wretched? Or else *according to the time* is referred to what follows, *died*: so that the sense is, he died according to the time, that is, for the three days of his burial. As if he said: this is very great and wonderful, that Christ deigned to die for us, weak and ungodly, since he himself is [[1 Cor 1:24|the power of God|virtus Dei]] and the Holy of Holies.

paras.t: Causam vero cur istud ita mirabile sit, subdit. Vix enim, id est raro et difficulter, pro justo a morte eruendo, quis moritur. Pauci enim sunt qui amore seu vice justi mori dignarentur. Et merito dixi, Vix, et non absolute, Nequaquam, vel, Non: nam pro bono, id est pro homine justo, forsitan quis audeat mori: id est, contingere potest, raro tamen, ut quis pro justo mori consentiat; sed ut quis pro impio mori velit, non invenitur, aut certe rarissime. Ambrosius (inter justum et bonum distinguens, ut justus dicatur qui in virtutibus exercitatus est, et in observatione justitiæ strenuus atque severus, bonus vero dicatur homo simplex et innocens, nondum sic exercitatus) ita exponit: Vix enim pro justo sic accepto quis moritur. Nam quamvis melior sit eo qui hoc modo bonus vocatur, quoniam tamen non sine rigore et severitate se habet, causa ejus minus miserabilis, seu miseratione minus condigna judicatur. Et veraciter dixi, pro justo quempiam vix velle mori: nam pro bono, id est pro pio, innocente et simplici, forsitan quis audeat mori, eo quod causa ejus miserabilior reputetur, tanquam qui nullum offendit. Quum ergo hoc raro inveniatur, certum est quod vix aliquis pro justo mori acquiescat.
paras.en: He adds the reason why this is so wonderful. [[5:7|For scarce|Vix enim]], that is, rarely and with difficulty, [[5:7|for a just man|pro justo]], to rescue him from death, [[5:7|will one die|quis moritur]]. For there are few who would deign to die out of love for a just man or in his stead. And rightly did I say *scarce*, and not absolutely *by no means*, or *not*: [[5:7|yet perhaps for a good man some one would dare to die|nam pro bono forsitan quis audeat mori]], *for a good man*, that is, for a just man; that is, it can happen, though rarely, that someone consents to die for a just man; but that someone should be willing to die for an ungodly man is not found, or certainly very rarely. Ambrose (distinguishing between the just and the good, so that he is called just who is practised in the virtues and strenuous and severe in the keeping of justice, while he is called good who is simple and innocent, not yet so practised) explains it thus: *For scarce for a just man*, so taken, *will one die*. For although he is better than one who is called good in this way, yet since he does not carry himself without rigour and severity, his cause is judged less pitiable, or less deserving of pity. And truly did I say that one will scarcely be willing to die for a just man: *yet perhaps for a good man*, that is, for one who is devout, innocent and simple, *some one would dare to die*, because his cause is thought more pitiable, as one who has offended no one. Since, then, even this is rarely found, it is certain that scarcely anyone would consent to die for a just man.

paras.t: Quum igitur Christus pro impiis mori dignatus sit, recte subjungitur: Commendat autem, id est, commendabilem sive laudabilem ostendit, Deus Pater vel Trinitas, caritatem suam in nobis, id est, quam habet ad nos, et qua diligit nos per effectum suæ eximiæ pietatis; quoniam quum adhuc peccatores essemus, id est jugo vitiorum subjecti, et vinculis peccatorum irretiti, nec ab originali peccato redempti, secundum tempus Christi passionem præcedens, id est, antequam Christus mortuus fuit pro nobis. Loquitur enim Apostolus in persona generis humani, cujus multa individua tempus passionis Christi præcesserunt: et tunc erant, in quorum persona hoc dicit Apostolus. Vel, Secundum tempus, id est tri […] Christus pro nobis mortuus est, id est, mori dignatus, ut mortificati carne, vivificatique spiritu, serviamus illi in sanctitate atque justitia. In quo refulget inæstimabilis caritas Dei Patris ad nos, juxta illud Joannis: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret. Et Apostolus: Propter nimiam, inquit, caritatem suam qua dilexit nos, Deus Pater Filium suum misit. Multo igitur magis justificati nunc in sanguine ipsius, id est, quia Christus pro nobis mortuus est quum adhuc iniqui eramus, infirmi et peccatores, multo amplius nunc facta nostra reconciliatione ac liberatione justificati, id est a vitiis expurgati, gratiamque adepti per effusionem sanguinis Christi, salvi erimus ab ira, id est a damnatione æterna, per ipsum, videlicet Christum, seu merito ejus. Amplius enim est impium justificare, quam justificatum a pœna eruere.
